pronunciation-spelling.title_tr: Pronunciation and Spelling (Accents, Silent Letters, Liaison)
pronunciation-spelling.intro_tr: French spelling uses five accent marks (é, è, ê, ë, ç) that can change a vowel's sound, distinguish otherwise identical words, or mark a letter that disappeared centuries ago. A large number of letters; especially final consonants and the final -e; are simply silent, so written French is often "longer" than spoken French. Liaison is the process of pronouncing a normally silent final consonant when the next word starts with a vowel sound, which is what gives French its smooth, connected rhythm. Elision is a related phenomenon: certain short words drop their final vowel and add an apostrophe before a word starting with a vowel sound (le + ami → l'ami). Because French spelling rarely matches pronunciation one-to-one, these rules must be memorized early; getting them wrong is one of the most common signs of a beginner accent.

examples.translation_tr: I'm not hungry, but I'm thirsty.
examples.note_tr: Elision: ne + ai → n'ai, je + ai → j'ai. 'Faim' contains the nasal vowel [fɛ̃].

gender-of-nouns.intro_tr: Every French noun has a grammatical gender; masculine (masculin) or feminine (féminin); and this affects the article, adjective forms, and pronouns used with it. Unlike English, gender in French is not usually tied to biological sex for objects and ideas; it's a fixed grammatical property you must learn with each noun (best memorized together with its article: "le livre", not just "livre"). Word endings give reliable statistical hints about gender in a large majority of cases, but there are important, high-frequency exceptions that simply must be memorized. For people and animals, many nouns have distinct masculine and feminine forms built through predictable (and some irregular) suffix changes. Gender also drives agreement throughout the sentence: articles, adjectives, past participles, and some pronouns all change form to match the noun's gender.

definite-indefinite-articles.intro_tr: French nouns are almost always preceded by an article, and unlike English, that article must agree in gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural) with the noun it introduces. The definite articles (le, la, les; "the") are used for specific or known things, as well as for general/abstract concepts and likes/dislikes, where English often uses no article at all. The indefinite articles (un, une, des; "a/an/some") introduce unspecified, countable items. Both le and la shrink to l' before a vowel sound or a mute h, and un/une/des change to de (or d') after a negation. Mastering these small words is essential because they carry gender information that adjectives and pronouns later depend on.

plural-forms.intro_tr: In French, most nouns form their plural simply by adding -s to the singular, exactly like in English; but this final -s is almost always SILENT in speech, so the plural is usually signaled by the article (le → les, un → des) rather than by the noun's ending. Beyond the basic -s rule, several groups of nouns follow their own patterns: nouns ending in -eau, -eu, or -au typically add -x instead of -s, and most nouns ending in -al switch to -aux. A noun already ending in -s, -x, or -z in the singular does not change at all in the plural. Because so many of these plural markers are silent or invisible in casual speech, learners should focus on memorizing the WRITTEN rules below and on recognizing plurality through the article/determiner in spoken French.

subject-pronouns.intro_tr: Subject pronouns (pronoms sujets) are the small words; je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles; that tell you WHO is doing the action of the verb; in French they are almost never omitted, unlike in some languages, because the verb form alone doesn't always make the subject clear. French has both a singular and plural 'you' (tu vs. vous), and a formal/informal distinction that English no longer marks. The pronoun 'on' is especially important: in spoken French it is used constantly to mean 'we', even though grammatically it behaves like 'he/she/it' (3rd person singular). Gender matters for the 3rd person: il/ils for masculine, elle/elles for feminine, and 'ils' is the default for any mixed group. Getting these pronouns right; and knowing when 'je' must contract to 'j''; is one of the very first building blocks of French sentences.

etre-avoir.intro_tr: Être ("to be") and avoir ("to have") are the two most important verbs in French: both are highly irregular, both are used constantly in everyday speech, and both later serve as the auxiliary verbs for compound tenses like the passé composé. Être expresses identity, nationality, profession, characteristics, location, and time, while avoir expresses possession, age, and; crucially; many physical/emotional states that English expresses with "to be" (hungry, cold, afraid, right, etc.). Because their conjugations don't follow the regular -er/-ir/-re patterns, they simply have to be memorized from the start. Getting comfortable with these two verbs is the single most important first step in French, since almost every sentence eventually depends on one of them.

er-verbs-present.intro_tr: Regular -er verbs form the largest group of French verbs and follow the most predictable pattern in the present tense: drop the -er from the infinitive and add a fixed set of endings to the stem. This single pattern lets you conjugate hundreds of verbs (parler, aimer, habiter, travailler, and more) as soon as you memorize it. Some -er verbs need small spelling adjustments (like commencer or manger) purely to preserve pronunciation, not because the logic changes. Because four of the six forms (je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles) sound identical when spoken, listening comprehension relies heavily on context and subject pronouns rather than the verb ending itself.

ir-re-verbs-present.intro_tr: French verbs fall into three conjugation groups by infinitive ending, and this page covers the two trickier ones: -ir verbs and -re verbs. Regular -ir verbs (the "2nd group," like finir) insert the characteristic -iss- before the plural endings. -re verbs (the "3rd group," like vendre) drop the -re and add short endings, with no extra letter in the il/elle/on form. However, many very common -ir and -re verbs are irregular: some -ir verbs (partir, sortir, dormir) use a short stem with no -iss-, others (ouvrir, offrir) borrow -er endings entirely, and several -re verbs (prendre, mettre, dire, connaître) have their own quirks. Because irregularities are frequent here, the safest approach is to memorize each verb's full pattern rather than guessing from the infinitive alone.

tables.caption_tr: Present Tense Endings Overview by Verb Pattern
footnotes_tr: The short-stem -ir group drops the last consonant of the infinitive stem in the singular (par-t-ir → je pars, not je parts).
The -ir-like-er group (ouvrir, offrir, souffrir, découvrir) is a small but very common exception; do not add -is/-it endings to these verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Regular -ir Verbs (2nd Group); the finir Pattern
footnotes_tr: This is the most productive -ir pattern: most new or less common -ir verbs (e.g. rougir, agir, punir, remplir) follow it.
Notice the -iss- infix appears only in the plural forms (nous, vous, ils/elles), never in the singular.

tables.caption_tr: Regular -re Verbs (3rd Group); the vendre Pattern
footnotes_tr: In the il/elle/on form, the stem's final -d is simply kept with no added ending: it is NOT pronounced.
Other verbs in this pattern: descendre, entendre, rendre, dépendre, correspondre.

tables.caption_tr: Irregular Short-Stem -ir Verbs; the partir Pattern
footnotes_tr: The plural stem keeps the full consonant (part-, sort-, dorm-, sent-, serv-) while the singular stem drops the final consonant of that plural stem.
mentir (to lie) follows the same pattern: je mens, nous mentons.

tables.caption_tr: -ir Verbs Conjugated Like Regular -er Verbs; the ouvrir Pattern
footnotes_tr: A small closed group, but all four verbs are frequent; memorize them as a set.
Also includes couvrir (to cover) and its compounds.

tables.caption_tr: Common Irregular -re Verbs
footnotes_tr: prendre: drops the 'd' before -ons/-ez and doubles the 'n' before -ent (nous prenons, ils prennent). apprendre and comprendre follow the same pattern.
dire: the vous form is dites, not disez; a well-known exception (compare vous êtes, vous faites).
connaître: takes a circumflex on the 'î' whenever it is followed by 't' (il connaît, but nous connaissons has no circumflex). paraître and disparaître follow the same rule.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Quick Tips
rows: Only 2nd-group verbs like finir take -iss-; partir, sortir, dormir never do.
ouvrir, offrir, souffrir, découvrir use -er endings, not -ir endings.
Forgetting nous/vous irregular forms of dire
vous dites is the odd one out; nous disons is regular.
Pronouncing the final -d/-t in -re/-ir singular forms
The final consonant of il/elle/on forms (vend, part, dort) is silent.
il vend [von]; the 'd' is not pronounced
Check the meaning/verb family, not just the -ir ending, to pick the right pattern.
je sors (NOT je sortis in the present) vs je finis

negation-ne-pas.intro_tr: The standard way to negate a French sentence is to place the conjugated verb inside a two-part frame: ne ... pas. In simple tenses, ne comes right before the conjugated verb and pas right after it; in compound tenses (like passé composé), the frame surrounds the auxiliary verb (avoir/être), while the past participle stays outside, after pas. Ne shrinks to n' before a vowel sound or a mute h, and in casual spoken French it is very frequently dropped altogether, leaving pas to carry the negation alone. A key trap for learners: after a negative sentence, the indefinite articles (un, une, des) and the partitive articles (du, de la, de l') almost always collapse into a simple de (or d').

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: ne + verb + pas (Present Tense, parler)
footnotes_tr: The verb between ne and pas is always the CONJUGATED verb, never an infinitive that follows it.

tables.caption_tr: Negation Across Different Tenses and Structures
rows: I am not going to eat.
Il m'a dit de ne pas manger.
He told me not to eat.
footnotes_tr: In compound tenses, only the auxiliary is inside the ne...pas frame; the past participle always comes after pas.
Object and reflexive pronouns always stay glued to the verb, inside the ne...pas frame.

tables.caption_tr: Elision and Reduction Rules for ne
rows: Je ne hais pas cette idée.
footnotes_tr: Dropping 'ne' is common in fast, informal spoken French but is considered incorrect in writing and formal speech.

tables.caption_tr: Article Changes After Negation: un/une/des/du/de la → de
rows: Je ne mange pas de pain.
Je ne bois pas de limonade.
footnotes_tr: This 'de' rule applies mainly to direct objects of avoir/manger/boire-type verbs.
Exception: after the verb être (to be), the article does NOT change to de; compare the last row.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with ne ... pas
rows: In writing/formal speech, 'ne' cannot be dropped; it must appear before the verb.
After negation, un/une/des/du/de la normally become plain 'de'.
'pas' goes AFTER the conjugated verb, never before it.
Je ne veux pas manger pas.
Only one 'pas' is needed; it wraps around the conjugated modal verb, not the infinitive.
'ne' must directly precede the conjugated verb, not stand at the very start of the clause with the subject after it.

question-formation.intro_tr: French has three main ways to turn a statement into a yes/no question, ranging from very informal to very formal, and they all follow the same word order rule for questions that ask for specific information: the question word goes first. The easiest method, rising intonation, just adds a question mark and a rising pitch to a normal statement, with no word-order change at all; perfect for casual conversation. The neutral, all-purpose method inserts "est-ce que" at the front of the sentence and is safe to use in speech or writing with anyone. The most formal method, inversion, swaps the verb and subject pronoun (and sometimes adds a linking "-t-"), and is typical of written French, polite requests, and set phrases. This sheet also covers interrogative words (où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien, qui, que, quel), the special inversion rules for noun subjects, and how to answer negative questions correctly with "si" instead of "oui".

tables.caption_tr: The Three Ways to Ask a Yes/No Question
rows: Subject + Verb + ? (rising pitch at the end, no word-order change)
Very informal; spoken French only, casual conversation
Est-ce que tu aimes le café ?
Neutral; works everywhere, safest choice for beginners
Formal; written French, polite speech, set expressions

tables.caption_tr: Interrogative Words (Question Words)
rows: Que fais-tu ? / Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?
How many brothers do you have?

tables.caption_tr: Question Word + Sentence: Three Register Options
rows: Statement word order + question word at the end
Question word + est-ce que + subject + verb

tables.caption_tr: Inversion Rules in Detail
rows: Pronoun subject (il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles)
Invert verb and pronoun directly, joined by a hyphen
Inversion with 'je' is awkward/rare in speech; prefer est-ce que; except a few fixed forms
Est-ce que je peux entrer ? ; but: Puis-je entrer ? (fixed, formal)
Verb ends in a vowel + subject il / elle / on
Insert -t- between the verb and the pronoun for pronunciation
Parle-t-il français ? ; A-t-elle un chat ? ; Va-t-on au parc ?
Keep the noun first, then invert the verb with a matching subject pronoun after it
Marie aime-t-elle le chocolat ? ; Pierre part-il demain ?
Object pronoun stays right before the verb; only the subject inverts
Only the auxiliary (avoir/être) inverts with the subject; past participle stays after

tables.caption_tr: Answering Yes/No Questions: oui, non, si
rows: Affirmative or negative question, negative answer
Negative question, but the answer is actually positive (contradicting the negative)
Tu n'aimes pas le café ?; Si, j'adore ça !
Don't you like coffee?; Yes, I love it!

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: Missing the hyphen and the required -t- link is not the issue here; the hyphen is mandatory in inversion
Verb ends in a vowel + 'il' needs a linking -t- for pronunciation
'Est-ce que' is never hyphenated between 'ce' and 'que'
Tu n'aimes pas le café ?; Oui.
'Oui' cannot contradict a negative question; use 'si' when the true answer is positive
Tu n'aimes pas le café ?; Si, j'adore ça.

numbers-time.intro_tr: French numbers are built by addition and multiplication rather than having a unique word for every value: 17 is literally "ten-seven" (dix-sept) and 80 is "four twenties" (quatre-vingts). A few numbers agree in gender or take a plural -s under specific conditions (vingt, cent), while others (mille) never change. Telling time uses two parallel systems: an everyday conversational style with "et quart / et demie / moins le quart" and an official 24-hour style used for schedules, where minutes are simply stated after the hour. Small agreement traps; un/une before feminine nouns like "heure", and when to add "de" after million/milliard; trip up beginners constantly, so this page groups every rule and exception into reference tables you can scan quickly.

tables.caption_tr: Cardinal Numbers 0–20
rows: un (masc.) / une (fem.); the only number that agrees in gender
pronounced [sis] alone, [siz] before vowel, [si] before consonant
silent h; liaison as [t] before vowel
in 'neuf ans/heures' the f sounds like [v]
final -t silent alone, pronounced in vingt et un, vingt-deux...

tables.caption_tr: Numbers 20–100: The Tens
Numbers 70–99 in Detail (Standard French)
footnotes_tr: In Belgium and Switzerland: 70 = septante, 90 = nonante (both regions); 80 = huitante in Switzerland (some cantons) but quatre-vingts remains standard in Belgium and France.
'Et' appears only with 1 in compounds of 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, and 71 (soixante et onze); it is never used with 81 or 91 (quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze).

tables.caption_tr: Large Numbers: Hundreds, Thousands, Millions
rows: no article before 'un': just 'cent', not 'un cent'
cent takes -s when multiplied and not followed by another number
a noun; requires 'de' before another noun: un million d'habitants
also a noun; un milliard de dollars

rows: irregular; only ordinal with a distinct feminine form beyond -e

The 24-hour system is standard for timetables, TV/radio schedules, and formal writing; the 12-hour 'et quart / moins le quart' system dominates everyday speech.

'mille' is invariable and never takes -s, even in the plural

'heure' must be plural after any number greater than one

adjective-agreement.intro_tr: In French, adjectives are not fixed words; they change form to match the gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural) of the noun they describe, and this is called agreement. Most adjectives simply add -e for the feminine and -s for the plural, but many common adjectives follow special patterns (like -eux→-euse or -al→-aux) that you need to memorize. Unlike English, most French adjectives are placed AFTER the noun (une voiture rouge), but a small, frequent group of short adjectives (covering Beauty, Age, Goodness, and Size; remembered with the acronym BAGS) go BEFORE the noun (une belle voiture). A handful of adjectives even change meaning depending on whether they come before or after the noun, so word order is not just a style choice; it can change what you're saying.

bleu clair, vert foncé, bleu marine

possessive-adjectives.intro_tr: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his/her, our, their) tell us who owns something, but in French they don't just depend on the owner; they must agree in gender and number with the noun being possessed. This is the single biggest trap for English speakers: "his book" and "her book" are both "son livre" in French, because "livre" is masculine, and the adjective agrees with "livre," not with "he" or "she." There is also a small but essential pronunciation rule: before a feminine singular noun that starts with a vowel or a mute h, "ma/ta/sa" are replaced by "mon/ton/son" purely to avoid an awkward vowel clash. Master the full paradigm below and this becomes automatic.

tables.caption_tr: Full Paradigm of French Possessive Adjectives
Key Rule: French Agrees with the THING Owned, Not the Owner
rows: 'livre' is masculine → always 'son', no matter who owns it
'voiture' is feminine → always 'sa', no matter who owns it
'amis' is plural → always 'ses', no matter who owns it
Never think 'his' = masculine form; think of the noun's gender only

tables.caption_tr: The Vowel-Sound Exception: mon/ton/son Replace ma/ta/sa
rows: This is purely for sound (to avoid a vowel clash); the noun is still grammatically feminine.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes & Quick Fixes
rows: Using 'ma' before a feminine noun starting with a vowel
Creates an awkward vowel clash (ma école)
Choosing possessive based on the owner's gender (e.g., 'sa' for 'his' because 'he' feels masculine)
French agreement is with the possessed noun, not the owner
son / sa / ses; determined by the noun's gender & number
Using 'leur' for a plural possessed noun
'leur' is singular; only the possessed noun's number matters, not the number of owners
leurs clés (keys, plural) vs. leur clé (key, singular)
'notre' and 'votre' are for singular possessed nouns only
'son' family = one owner; 'leur' family = multiple owners
Marie prend son sac (her bag) vs. Marie et Paul prennent leur sac (their bag)

aller-venir.title_tr: Aller and Venir; The Near Future (aller + infinitive)
aller-venir.intro_tr: Aller (to go) and venir (to come) are two of the most frequently used irregular verbs in French, essential for talking about movement, direction, and well-being. Both verbs are highly irregular in the present tense; despite aller ending in -er, it does not follow the regular -er pattern at all; so their forms must simply be memorized. Beyond describing physical movement, these two verbs combine with an infinitive to build two of the most useful everyday time expressions in French: the futur proche (aller + infinitive) for the near future ("going to do something") and the passé récent (venir de + infinitive) for the recent past ("just did something"). Learning these patterns early lets you talk naturally about upcoming and just-completed actions long before you need the full future or past tenses. Both verbs also take être (not avoir) as their auxiliary in the passé composé, a detail worth remembering for later lessons.

tables.caption_tr: Aller ("to go"); Present Tense, Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: Aller looks like a regular -er verb in the infinitive but is completely irregular in conjugation; the stem changes in almost every form.
In the passé composé, aller takes être as its auxiliary and agrees with the subject: je suis allé(e), elle est allée, ils sont allés.

tables.caption_tr: Venir ("to come"); Present Tense, Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: Venir also takes être in the passé composé: je suis venu(e), elles sont venues.
Verbs built on venir (devenir 'to become', revenir 'to come back', se souvenir 'to remember') and the tenir family (tenir, obtenir, maintenir) follow the exact same irregular pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Futur Proche: aller (conjugated) + Infinitive; "going to do something"
footnotes_tr: The infinitive never changes form regardless of subject; only aller is conjugated.
The futur proche is the most common way to talk about the future in spoken French, often preferred over the futur simple for near or planned events.
Negation wraps around aller only: je ne vais pas partir (I am not going to leave).

tables.caption_tr: Passé Récent: venir de (conjugated) + Infinitive; "to have just done something"
footnotes_tr: 'de' contracts to d' before a vowel sound or a mute h: elle vient d'arriver, ils viennent d'habiter ici.
The passé récent describes an action completed in the very recent past, relative to now (or to another reference point in the past when using imparfait: je venais de sortir = I had just gone out).

tables.caption_tr: Aller + à + Place: Required Contractions
rows: I am going to the movies.
I am going to the pool.
I am going to the restroom.
footnotes_tr: These contractions are obligatory in French; you can never say 'à le' or 'à les'.
The same contraction rules apply after any verb followed by à + a definite article, not only aller.

tables.caption_tr: Common Idiomatic Expressions with Aller and Venir
rows: This hat goes well to you
This hat suits you / looks good on you.
to leave, to go away (reflexive form of aller)
to indicate origin: Je viens de Londres.
to come to look for someone
to send for / summon someone (a doctor, a repairman, etc.)
footnotes_tr: 'aller' meaning 'to suit/fit' (clothing, colors) is a very common everyday use distinct from physical movement.
s'en aller is more emphatic/dramatic than simply 'partir' and is common in spoken French and songs (e.g., 'Je m'en vais').

partitive-articles.intro_tr: Partitive articles (du, de la, de l', des) are used in French to express an unspecified quantity or "some/any" amount of something; typically mass nouns like food, drinks, and abstract qualities that cannot be counted individually. They contrast with definite articles (le/la/les, used for specific things or general categories) and indefinite articles (un/une/des, used for countable whole items). In negative sentences, every partitive form collapses to simply "de" (or "d'" before a vowel sound). Because English has no true equivalent (it's often just left untranslated, or rendered loosely as "some"), learners frequently either omit the article entirely or confuse it with the indefinite article; mastering this distinction is essential for natural-sounding French.

tables.caption_tr: Forms of the Partitive Article
rows: de l'eau (water), de l'argent (money), de l'huile (oil)

tables.caption_tr: Partitive vs. Definite vs. Indefinite Articles
rows: du, de la, de l', des
an unspecified quantity/part of an uncountable thing
Je mange du pain. (I eat some bread.)
specific known things, or general categories/likes-dislikes
J'aime le pain. (I like bread [in general].)
Je mange un pain. (I eat a loaf of bread.)
footnotes_tr: Note: plural 'des' looks identical for both partitive and indefinite plural, but the meaning shifts depending on whether the noun is countable (indefinite) or a mass/collective idea (partitive).

tables.caption_tr: Partitive Articles in Negative Sentences
rows: Je ne bois pas de café.
Elle ne mange pas de viande.
footnotes_tr: Exception: after the verb être, the partitive keeps its full form even in the negative; 'Ce n'est pas du vin' (This isn't wine), because être introduces an identity, not a quantity being negated.

tables.caption_tr: Expressions of Quantity Always Use de/d' (never du, de la, des)
rows: la plupart des gens (de + les → des)
footnotes_tr: This 'de' is invariable; it does not agree in gender/number and never becomes du/de la/des, except when the following noun already has its own definite article (la plupart des gens).

tables.caption_tr: Typical Nouns Used with the Partitive (Mass Nouns)
rows: du pain, du fromage, de la viande, du poisson, de la salade
de l'eau, du café, du thé, du vin, de la bière
du courage, de la patience, de la chance, du temps, de l'énergie
il y a du vent, il y a du soleil, il y a de la neige

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Partitive Articles
rows: Je ne veux pas du café.
Je ne veux pas de café.
After a negation, du/de la/de l'/des must become de (or d').
Countable single items take the indefinite article (un/une), not the partitive.
Je mange du pain le matin.
French virtually always requires an article before a noun; it cannot be dropped as in English.
Before a vowel or mute h, both masculine and feminine nouns use de l', not de la.
Il boit de l'eau. / Il boit des eaux (minérales).
Don't pluralize an uncountable singular noun just because 'des' looks plural; use de l' for the mass-noun meaning.

examples.translation_tr: I eat (some) bread every morning.

examples.target: Elle boit de la limonade.
examples.translation_tr: She drinks (some) lemonade.

examples.target: Nous avons de l'argent pour le voyage.
examples.translation_tr: We have (some) money for the trip.

examples.target: Ils achètent des fraises au marché.
examples.translation_tr: They buy (some) strawberries at the market.

examples.target: Je ne mange pas de viande.
examples.translation_tr: I don't eat (any) meat.

examples.target: Elle a beaucoup de patience avec les enfants.

prepositions-basic.title_tr: Basic Prepositions (à, de, en, chez) and Contractions (au, du)
prepositions-basic.intro_tr: French uses a small set of workhorse prepositions; à, de, en, and chez; to express location, direction, origin, possession, and time, but their meanings shift depending on context, so they must be learned use by use rather than translated word-for-word. A crucial mechanical rule sits alongside them: à and de are never allowed to sit directly in front of the definite articles le or les; they must fuse into single contracted words (au, aux, du, des). No contraction happens with la or l', which is the single most common beginner mistake to watch for. Because à and de also govern how countries and cities are introduced (à Paris vs. en France vs. au Japon), this topic doubles as your foundation for talking about location and travel. Master the contraction table first; it appears in almost every French sentence you will ever produce.

tables.caption_tr: Contraction Rules: à / de + Definite Article
footnotes_tr: Contraction is MANDATORY with le and les; you can never write 'à le' or 'de les'.
No contraction happens with la or l'; 'à la', 'à l'', 'de la', 'de l'' stay as two separate words.
'des' here is the contraction of de+les; it looks identical to the plural indefinite article 'des' (some), but the two have different origins and functions.

tables.caption_tr: Core Uses of à
rows: Le village est à 5 km d'ici.
The village is 5 km from here.
à pied, à vélo, à la main
on foot, by bike, by hand

tables.caption_tr: Core Uses of de
rows: Content or material inside a container
Describing what something is for/made of type
parler de, avoir besoin de, avoir peur de
to talk about, to need, to be afraid of
beaucoup de temps, un peu de sucre
a lot of time, a bit of sugar

tables.caption_tr: Core Uses of en
rows: en voiture, en train, en avion
by car, by train, by plane
Time it takes to complete something
Il a fini en deux heures.
en vacances, en retard, en forme
on vacation, late, in good shape

tables.caption_tr: Core Uses of chez
rows: I have an appointment at the doctor's.
Within a group, culture, or author's work
This is common among the French.

tables.caption_tr: Prepositions with Places: Cities and Countries
rows: Il habite à Rome. / Il vient de Rome.
Feminine country (ends in -e, e.g. la France)
Elle vit en Espagne. / Elle vient d'Espagne.
Il travaille au Japon. / Il rentre du Japon.
Ils étudient aux États-Unis. / Ils viennent des États-Unis.
Masculine country starting with a vowel (e.g. l'Iran)
Elle voyage en Iran. / Elle revient d'Iran.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Look-Alikes
rows: à + le must always fuse into 'au'.
'en' is used in many fixed abstract expressions; 'dans' usually needs a concrete container or a specific time-in-the-future sense (dans deux jours = in two days from now).
Each verb fixes its own preposition (penser à, parler de); these must be memorized per verb, not guessed.
Cities use à; most countries need en/au/aux depending on gender and number.

examples.target: Je vais au cinéma ce soir.
examples.translation_tr: I'm going to the cinema tonight. (à + le → au)

examples.target: Elle habite à Paris, en France.
examples.translation_tr: She lives in Paris, in France. (à = city, en = feminine country)

examples.target: Le livre est sur la table du salon.
examples.translation_tr: The book is on the living room's table. (de + le → du)

examples.target: Nous allons chez nos grands-parents ce week-end.
examples.translation_tr: We're going to our grandparents' place this weekend.

examples.target: Il parle aux étudiants avant l'examen.
examples.translation_tr: He speaks to the students before the exam. (à + les → aux)

examples.target: Je reviens des États-Unis demain.
examples.translation_tr: I'm coming back from the United States tomorrow. (de + les → des)

examples.target: Elle boit un café au lait le matin.
examples.translation_tr: She drinks coffee with milk in the morning. (au = with, in this fixed expression)

examples.target: Le professeur explique la leçon aux élèves de la classe.
examples.translation_tr: The teacher explains the lesson to the students of the class. (aux + de la in one sentence)

passe-compose-avoir.intro_tr: The passé composé is the most frequently used past tense in spoken French, expressing completed actions ("I ate", "she has finished", "we went"). It is a compound tense built from two parts: an auxiliary verb in the present tense (either avoir or être) plus the past participle of the main verb. The large majority of French verbs; all transitive verbs and most intransitive ones; take avoir as their auxiliary; only about seventeen verbs of movement/state plus all reflexive verbs use être instead (see the related topic). This page focuses entirely on the avoir pattern: how to conjugate avoir, how to form regular and irregular past participles, and how word order shifts in negative and question forms.

tables.caption_tr: Basic structure of the passé composé with avoir
rows: je, tu, il/elle/on, nous, vous, ils/elles
Il a mangé. (He ate / He has eaten.)
footnotes_tr: A single passé composé form corresponds to three English translations: 'I ate', 'I have eaten', 'I did eat'.

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation of avoir in the present tense (the auxiliary)
footnotes_tr: Note the elision: je + ai → j'ai. This is the only person where elision occurs with avoir.

tables.caption_tr: Regular past participle formation by verb group
footnotes_tr: -er verbs are almost entirely regular and predictable: infinitive minus '-er' plus '-é'.
-ir verbs in this table are the regular type (like finir); many other -ir verbs are irregular (see next table).

tables.caption_tr: Common irregular past participles
rows: to be necessary (il faut → il a fallu)
to rain (il pleut → il a plu)
footnotes_tr: These must simply be memorized; there is no single reliable rule.
Note dû takes a circumflex only in the masculine singular, to distinguish it from the partitive article 'du'.

tables.caption_tr: Negative and question forms in the passé composé
rows: Subject + ne + avoir + pas + past participle
Je n'ai pas mangé. (I didn't eat.)
Subject + ne + avoir + jamais + past participle
Il n'a jamais voyagé. (He has never traveled.)
Subject + ne + avoir + rien + past participle
Elle n'a rien dit. (She didn't say anything.)
Est-ce que + subject + avoir + past participle
Est-ce que tu as mangé ? (Did you eat?)
footnotes_tr: The negation particles (pas, jamais, rien, plus) wrap around the auxiliary avoir, NOT around the past participle: ne + avoir + [negation word] + participle.
Compare: ne...personne and ne...que go AFTER the past participle instead: Il n'a vu personne. / Il n'a bu que de l'eau.

tables.caption_tr: Common time expressions used with the passé composé
footnotes_tr: These markers signal a completed, punctual action; a strong clue to use passé composé rather than imparfait.

examples.target: J'ai mangé une pomme.
examples.translation_tr: I ate an apple.

examples.target: Tu as regardé un film hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: You watched a movie last night.

examples.target: Il a fini ses devoirs avant le dîner.
examples.translation_tr: He finished his homework before dinner.

examples.target: Nous avons visité Paris l'année dernière.
examples.translation_tr: We visited Paris last year.

examples.target: Elle n'a pas compris la question.
examples.translation_tr: She didn't understand the question.

examples.target: Avez-vous déjà voyagé en France ?
examples.translation_tr: Have you ever traveled to France?

examples.target: Ils ont pris le train ce matin.
examples.translation_tr: They took the train this morning.

examples.target: J'ai eu peur pendant le film.
examples.translation_tr: I got scared during the movie.

passe-compose-etre.title_tr: Passé Composé with être and Past Participle Agreement
passe-compose-etre.intro_tr: A small but very frequent group of French verbs; mostly verbs of movement or state (aller, venir, partir, arriver, naître, mourir, etc.); form the passé composé with être instead of avoir. All reflexive (pronominal) verbs use être too. The key difference from avoir-verbs is that the past participle must AGREE in gender and number with the subject, just like an adjective: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural. A handful of these verbs (monter, descendre, sortir, passer, rentrer, retourner) can switch back to avoir when they take a direct object, and their meaning shifts slightly. Memorizing the list; often taught as "Dr & Mrs Vandertramp"; and the agreement rule together is essential for accurate written French.

tables.caption_tr: Present tense of être (the auxiliary verb used here)
The 'Dr & Mrs Vandertramp' verbs; the core group conjugated with être
Full conjugation example: aller (to go) with subject agreement
Past participle agreement rule with être; summary
rows: Ils sont partis. / Paul et Marie sont partis.
agrees with the real, implied subject
On est parti(e)(s).; agreement follows who 'on' refers to

tables.caption_tr: Verbs that change auxiliary (and meaning) between avoir and être
rows: Il est monté au premier étage. (He went up.)
Il a monté les valises. (He carried the suitcases up.)
Elle est descendue du taxi. (She got out.)
Elle a descendu l'escalier en courant. (She ran down the stairs.; object = l'escalier)
Nous sommes sortis ce soir. (We went out.)
Nous avons sorti le chien. (We took the dog out.)
Il est passé chez moi. (He stopped by my place.)
Il a passé un examen. (He took an exam.)
Elle est rentrée tard. (She got home late.)
Elle a rentré la voiture au garage. (She put the car back in the garage.)
Ils sont retournés à Rome. (They went back.)
Il a retourné la crêpe. (He flipped the pancake.)

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive (pronominal) verbs; a quick preview (always use être)
rows: il s'est levé / elle s'est levée
ils se sont levés / elles se sont levées

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with être + past participle
rows: Feminine subject needs -e on the past participle.
Plural subject needs -s on the past participle.
Marie a sortie avec ses amis.
Marie est sortie avec ses amis.
'sortir' with no direct object uses être, not avoir.
'monter' with no direct object uses être; 'a monté' is only correct with a direct object (e.g., monter les valises).
Nous sommes née à Lyon. (a man speaking)
Je suis né à Lyon. / Nous sommes nés à Lyon. (mixed/masc. group)
The participle must match the true gender/number of the subject, not just default to feminine.

examples.target: Elle est allée à Paris.
examples.translation_tr: She went to Paris.
examples.note_tr: Feminine subject → -e added to the past participle: allé → allée.

examples.target: Ils sont partis tôt ce matin.
examples.translation_tr: They left early this morning.
examples.note_tr: All-masculine (or mixed) plural subject → -s added: parti → partis.

examples.target: Nous sommes arrivées à l'heure.
examples.translation_tr: We arrived on time. (a group of women speaking)
examples.note_tr: Feminine plural 'nous' → -es added: arrivé → arrivées.

examples.target: Il est né en 1990 et il est mort en 2020.
examples.translation_tr: He was born in 1990 and he died in 2020.
examples.note_tr: naître → né and mourir → mort are irregular past participles.

examples.target: Je suis monté dans le train, mais j'ai monté les valises.
examples.translation_tr: I got on the train, but I carried the suitcases up.
examples.note_tr: monter with être = intransitive movement; monter with avoir + direct object = transitive action, meaning shifts.

examples.target: Vous êtes descendus du bus devant la gare.
examples.translation_tr: You got off the bus in front of the station.
examples.note_tr: 'vous' here is masculine plural → -s added: descendu → descendus.

examples.target: Marie et Paul sont sortis ensemble hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: Marie and Paul went out together last night.
examples.note_tr: Mixed-gender plural subject → the masculine plural form (-s) is used by default.

examples.target: Elle s'est levée à sept heures.
examples.translation_tr: She got up at seven o'clock.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive verbs also take être; the participle usually agrees with the reflexive pronoun (subject) here; full rules covered in the advanced agreement topic.

imparfait.title_tr: Imparfait: Continuity and Description in the Past
imparfait.intro_tr: The imparfait (imperfect) is a past tense used to describe ongoing situations, habits, and background scenery rather than single completed events. Unlike the passé composé, which reports finished actions with a clear beginning and end, the imparfait paints the "scenery" of the past: what things looked like, what people were doing, or what used to happen regularly. It is built from a single stem (mostly the nous-form of the present tense minus -ons) plus one fixed set of endings that works for every verb; including irregular ones; except être. Because it has no notion of completion, the imparfait is essential for storytelling, physical/mental descriptions, habitual actions, and polite, softened requests.

tables.caption_tr: Imparfait endings (identical for all verbs, attached to the imperfect stem)
footnotes_tr: Note: nous and vous forms end in -ions / -iez, which can sound identical to the present tense for -ier verbs (e.g., étudiions); the extra 'i' is a common spelling pitfall.
The -ais, -ais, -ait, -aient endings are all pronounced the same way: [ɛ].

tables.caption_tr: How to find the imperfect stem
rows: nous parlons / nous finissons / nous vendons
je parlais / je finissais / je vendais
être has an irregular stem: ét-
footnotes_tr: This stem-finding trick works for virtually every French verb, including irregular ones like faire (nous faisons → fais-) and boire (nous buvons → buv-).

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation across the three regular verb groups
Imperfect stems of key irregular verbs
footnotes_tr: être is the only truly irregular imperfect stem in French; all other verbs follow the nous-minus-ons rule even when their present tense is irregular.

tables.caption_tr: Main uses of the imparfait
rows: Something that used to happen regularly, with no fixed end
Chaque été, nous allions à la mer. (Every summer, we used to go to the sea.)
Painting a static picture of how things were
Le village était calme et paisible. (The village was calm and peaceful.)
What was happening 'behind' the main event
Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. (It was raining when I went out.)
Used with passé composé: imparfait = the ongoing action, passé composé = the interruption
Je dormais quand tu as appelé. (I was sleeping when you called.)
Age, time, weather in the past
Standard way to state background facts
Il était trois heures et il faisait froid. (It was three o'clock and it was cold.)
Makes a request sound less direct
Je voulais vous poser une question. (I wanted to ask you a question.)
Hypothetical habitual condition (si + imparfait, in both clauses)
Describes what regularly used to happen under a condition
Si on avait le temps, on visitait le musée. (If we had time, we would visit the museum.)
A common conversational way to propose an idea
Et si on partait en week-end? (What if we went away for the weekend?)

tables.caption_tr: Imparfait vs. Passé Composé at a glance
rows: Describes an ongoing state or background situation
No clear beginning or end is expressed
Has a clear beginning and/or end
Sets the scene of a story
A change of state or a sudden event
Quand j'étais jeune, j'habitais à Rome. (ongoing state)
Hier, j'ai déménagé à Rome. (completed event)
footnotes_tr: Many sentences combine both: the imparfait describes the scene/background while the passé composé narrates what happened, e.g., Il faisait nuit quand nous sommes arrivés.

tables.caption_tr: Time expressions commonly paired with the imparfait
rows: tous les jours / tous les ans
Tous les jours, il se promenait au parc.
Autrefois, il n'y avait pas de voitures ici.
À cette époque-là, je vivais seul.
Quand j'étais petit, je détestais les légumes.
Chaque été, nous allions chez mes grands-parents.
footnotes_tr: These recurring-time expressions are strong signals that the imparfait (not the passé composé) is the correct choice, because they describe repeated or ongoing patterns rather than single events.

examples.target: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais dans le jardin tous les jours.
examples.translation_tr: When I was little, I used to play in the garden every day.
examples.note_tr: Habitual past action + description of childhood; classic imparfait context.

examples.target: Il faisait beau ce jour-là et les oiseaux chantaient.
examples.translation_tr: The weather was nice that day and the birds were singing.
examples.note_tr: Describing weather and an ongoing background scene.

examples.target: Elle lisait tranquillement quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.translation_tr: She was reading quietly when the phone rang.
examples.note_tr: Imparfait (ongoing background action) interrupted by passé composé (sudden event).

examples.target: Nous habitions à Lyon pendant dix ans avant de déménager à Paris.
examples.translation_tr: We lived in Lyon for ten years before moving to Paris.
examples.note_tr: A long, undefined-boundary state in the past; typical imparfait use.

examples.target: Tu avais les cheveux longs et tu portais toujours des lunettes.
examples.translation_tr: You had long hair and you always wore glasses.
examples.note_tr: Physical description in the past.

examples.target: D'habitude, mes grands-parents se levaient à six heures du matin.
examples.translation_tr: Usually, my grandparents used to get up at six in the morning.
examples.note_tr: Repeated habitual routine marked by 'd'habitude'.

examples.target: Je voulais vous demander un petit service, si c'est possible.
examples.translation_tr: I wanted to ask you a small favor, if that's possible.
examples.note_tr: Softened, polite request; imparfait de politesse.

examples.target: S'il pleuvait, nous restions à la maison toute la journée.
examples.translation_tr: If it rained, we would stay home all day.
examples.note_tr: Imparfait used in both clauses to express a habitual hypothetical situation in the past.

passe-compose-vs-imparfait.intro_tr: French has two common ways to talk about the past: passé composé and imparfait, and the tricky part is that English often uses the same simple past tense ("I ate", "I was eating", "I used to eat") for situations that French carefully distinguishes. As a rough rule, passé composé tells WHAT HAPPENED; a specific, completed event or a sequence of actions that move the story forward; while imparfait describes WHAT WAS GOING ON; background, description, habits, ongoing states, and the "scenery" of a story. The two tenses are not competitors that you pick one or the other for the whole story; they work together constantly, with imparfait painting the scene and passé composé placing events onto it. This page gives you the core rules, verbs whose meaning changes between the two tenses, and a decision checklist you can use every time you're not sure which one to pick.

tables.caption_tr: Core distinction: what each tense communicates
rows: A specific, completed action; a single event; a change of state; a sequence of events that push the story forward
hier, un jour, soudain, tout à coup, une fois, plusieurs fois, à ce moment-là, pendant + [specific duration ending now/known]
Description, background setting, ongoing/unfinished action, habitual or repeated action in the past, physical/mental states, age, weather, time
A line stretching across the timeline (, , )
autrefois, avant, chaque jour, tous les ans, souvent, d'habitude, toujours, quand j'étais + [age/state], pendant que

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation reminder: how each tense is formed
Imparfait endings (regular for all verbs except être stem)
The 'interrupted action' pattern
rows: Background action interrupted by a sudden event
Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné. (I was sleeping when the phone rang.)
Two ongoing actions happening simultaneously in the background
Pendant qu'il lisait, elle écrivait. (While he was reading, she was writing.)
Passé composé, puis passé composé, puis...
A chain of completed events moving the plot forward
Il s'est levé, a pris son café et est parti. (He got up, had his coffee, and left.)

tables.caption_tr: Verbs that change meaning depending on the tense
rows: j'ai su = I found out / I learned (moment of discovery)
je connaissais = I knew, was familiar with
j'ai connu = I met (for the first time) / I got to know
j'ai voulu = I decided to / tried to (and often: ai voulu = attempted; n'ai pas voulu = refused)
je pouvais = I was able to / had the ability (in general)
j'ai pu = I managed to / succeeded in (on that specific occasion)
je devais = I was supposed to (may or may not have happened)
j'ai dû = I had to (and did) / I must have (deduction)
j'ai été, j'ai eu = a state that began/ended at a specific moment, e.g. j'ai eu peur = I got scared

tables.caption_tr: Quick decision checklist
rows: Is it a description (weather, age, appearance, feelings, setting the scene)?
Is it a habit or something repeated regularly ('every day', 'always')?
Is it a single, completed event, or does it move the story to the next moment?
Is it an action interrupted by another action?
background = imparfait, interrupting event = passé composé
reconsider context; default to passé composé for finished actions with a clear endpoint

examples.target: Hier, je suis allé au marché et j'ai acheté des pommes.
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday, I went to the market and I bought some apples.
examples.note_tr: Both verbs are single, completed actions on the timeline → passé composé.

examples.target: Quand j'étais petit, j'allais à la plage tous les étés.
examples.translation_tr: When I was little, I used to go to the beach every summer.
examples.note_tr: Habitual, repeated action in the past + background state 'was little' → imparfait for both.

examples.target: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti de la maison.
examples.translation_tr: It was raining when I went out of the house.
examples.note_tr: Classic pattern: imparfait sets the background scene, passé composé interrupts it with a single event.

examples.target: Nous étions fatigués après le voyage.
examples.translation_tr: We were tired after the trip.
examples.note_tr: A description/state, not an action → imparfait.

examples.target: Soudain, le téléphone a sonné.
examples.translation_tr: Suddenly, the phone rang.
examples.note_tr: 'Soudain' signals a sudden, punctual event → passé composé.

examples.target: Elle regardait la télévision pendant que je faisais la cuisine.
examples.translation_tr: She was watching television while I was cooking.
examples.note_tr: Two parallel, ongoing background actions happening at the same time → imparfait for both.

examples.target: J'ai vécu à Paris pendant trois ans.
examples.translation_tr: I lived in Paris for three years.
examples.note_tr: A duration with clear start and end, treated as a completed block of time → passé composé, even though it lasted a while.

examples.target: Avant, je ne savais pas parler français, mais un jour j'ai décidé d'apprendre.
examples.translation_tr: Before, I didn't know how to speak French, but one day I decided to learn.
examples.note_tr: Ongoing past state (savais) contrasted with a single decisive moment (ai décidé).

reflexive-verbs.intro_tr: Reflexive (pronominal) verbs are verbs that appear together with a reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) that refers back to the subject, as in "se lever" (to get (oneself) up) or "s'appeler" (to call oneself / to be named). Many everyday actions related to daily routine; washing, dressing, waking up, going to bed; are expressed with reflexive verbs in French even when the English equivalent has no "-self". Some reflexive verbs like "se lever" and "s'appeler" also undergo the same spelling changes (é→è, consonant doubling) as their non-reflexive -er verb relatives. In compound tenses, ALL reflexive verbs are conjugated with the auxiliary "être", and the past participle usually agrees with the subject; unless a direct object appears after the verb. Beyond true reflexive meaning ("oneself"), pronominal verbs can also express reciprocity ("each other"), a fixed idiomatic meaning, or a passive-like sense.

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive pronouns (one for every subject)
footnotes_tr: The reflexive pronoun always sits directly before the conjugated verb (except in the affirmative imperative).
Elision (me→m', te→t', se→s') happens before a verb starting with a vowel or a mute 'h', e.g. je m'habille.

tables.caption_tr: Present tense; se lever (stem-changing: é → è), 'to get up'
footnotes_tr: The stem vowel changes from 'e' to 'è' in every form except nous and vous (the classic 'boot/shoe' pattern), because those endings are unstressed 'mute e' syllables.
Other verbs following this exact pattern: se promener (to take a walk), s'acheter (to buy oneself), se peser (to weigh oneself).

tables.caption_tr: Present tense; s'appeler (consonant doubling: l → ll), 'to be named / call oneself'
rows: I am named / my name is
footnotes_tr: The final consonant of the stem doubles (l → ll) in every form except nous and vous, for the same pronunciation reason as se lever.
Other verbs with the same doubling pattern: se rappeler (to recall), jeter-type verbs double 't' (e.g. se projeter → il se projette).

tables.caption_tr: Present tense; se laver (regular -er reflexive model, no spelling change), 'to wash oneself'
footnotes_tr: Most reflexive -er verbs (s'habiller, se reposer, se dépêcher, se demander...) follow this fully regular pattern with no internal spelling change.

tables.caption_tr: Negation with reflexive verbs: ne + reflexive pronoun + verb + pas
footnotes_tr: 'ne' comes before the reflexive pronoun, and 'pas' comes after the conjugated verb: the reflexive pronoun stays glued to the verb, never split off by 'ne'.

tables.caption_tr: Passé composé of se lever; always with être, participle agrees with the subject
footnotes_tr: ALL reflexive verbs take 'être' as the auxiliary in compound tenses (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, etc.), never 'avoir'.
The past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject when the reflexive pronoun functions as the DIRECT object (the usual case).
EXCEPTION; no agreement when a direct object noun follows the verb: 'Elle s'est lavé les mains' (not 'lavée'), because 'les mains' is the direct object and 'se' is then indirect.

tables.caption_tr: Imperative (command) forms of se lever
footnotes_tr: Affirmative imperative: the reflexive pronoun moves AFTER the verb, joined by a hyphen, and 'te' becomes the stressed form 'toi'.
Negative imperative: the normal word order returns; ne + pronoun + verb + pas, with 'te' (not 'toi').

tables.caption_tr: Common reflexive verbs to know at A2 level
Four meanings of pronominal verbs: reflexive, reciprocal, idiomatic, and passive-like
rows: He washes himself.; the subject acts on itself.
They love each other.; two or more subjects act on one another.
Il se souvient de son enfance.
He remembers his childhood.; 'souvenir' does not exist alone with this meaning.
This book sells well.; equivalent to 'is sold well', no agent expressed.
footnotes_tr: Context and the type of subject (person vs. thing, singular vs. plural) usually make the intended meaning clear.

examples.target: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
examples.translation_tr: I get up at seven o'clock every day.

examples.target: Comment tu t'appelles ?
examples.translation_tr: What's your name? (informal 'tu')
examples.note_tr: 's'appeler' literally means 'to call oneself'; this is the standard way to ask someone's name informally.

examples.target: Elle s'est levée tôt ce matin.
examples.translation_tr: She got up early this morning.
examples.note_tr: Past participle 'levée' agrees with the feminine subject 'elle' because the reflexive pronoun 'se' acts as the direct object here.

examples.target: Nous nous couchons vers minuit.
examples.translation_tr: We go to bed around midnight.

examples.target: Dépêche-toi, on va être en retard !
examples.translation_tr: Hurry up, we're going to be late!
examples.note_tr: Affirmative imperative: the reflexive pronoun moves after the verb and 'te' becomes the stressed form 'toi'.

examples.target: Ils s'aiment depuis dix ans.
examples.translation_tr: They have loved each other for ten years.
examples.note_tr: Reciprocal use: 's'aimer' here means 'to love each other', not 'to love oneself'.

examples.target: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
examples.translation_tr: Don't worry, everything is fine.
examples.note_tr: Negative imperative: 'ne' + reflexive pronoun (unstressed 'te') + verb + 'pas'.

examples.target: Elle s'est lavé les mains avant de manger.
examples.translation_tr: She washed her hands before eating.
examples.note_tr: No agreement on 'lavé' here because 'les mains' (the hands) is the direct object placed after the verb; 'se' is only an indirect object in this sentence.

futur-simple.intro_tr: The futur simple is the standard "will do" future tense in French, used for predictions, promises, plans further ahead in time, and for events described as certain to happen. Unlike futur proche (aller + infinitive), which feels immediate and conversational, futur simple is the neutral, all-purpose future used in both speech and writing, and it is required after time conjunctions like quand, lorsque, dès que, and aussitôt que when referring to the future. Regular verbs are formed by adding one fixed set of endings (identical to the present tense of avoir: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont) directly to the infinitive, dropping the final -e for -re verbs. About seventeen very common verbs use an irregular stem that must simply be memorized, but the endings never change, even for irregular verbs. A key trap for beginners: with "si" (if) expressing a real condition, the si-clause itself stays in the present tense; the futur simple only appears in the result clause.

tables.caption_tr: Futur Simple Endings (added to the infinitive stem)
footnotes_tr: These endings are identical to the present-tense conjugation of avoir (ai, as, a, ons, ez, ont); a handy memory trick.
The stem for regular verbs is simply the infinitive; for -re verbs, drop the final -e before adding the endings.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation of Regular Verbs (one model per group)
footnotes_tr: Note that -ir and -er verbs look identical in futur simple except for one letter (parlera vs finira); listen for the vowel before the ending.

tables.caption_tr: Irregular Stems (endings stay completely regular)
footnotes_tr: Compounds of these verbs follow the same irregular stem: revenir → je reviendrai, devenir → je deviendrai, obtenir → j'obtiendrai, apercevoir → j'apercevrai, etc.
Note the double 'r' in many stems (courr-, mourr-, viendr-, verr-); this is what gives futur simple its characteristic sound, distinct from the conditionnel which uses the same stems.

tables.caption_tr: Spelling-Change Verbs in Futur Simple
rows: The grave accent appears throughout the conjugation, unlike some other tenses.
double the consonant in ALL persons
acheter-type: geler → je gèlerai; peler → je pèlerai
These behave like the -e_er group instead
nettoyer → je nettoierai; envoyer → j'enverrai (also irregular stem!)
payer → je paierai OR je payerai; essayer → j'essaierai OR j'essayerai
Both spellings are accepted in modern French

tables.caption_tr: Futur Simple vs. Futur Proche: When to Use Which
rows: Je vais partir dans cinq minutes.
Distant, vague, or less certain future
Un jour, je visiterai le Japon.
Il pleuvra demain sur toute la région.
After quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que + future meaning
In the result clause of a real 'si + present' condition
Si tu es libre, nous sortirons ensemble.
footnotes_tr: In everyday spoken French, futur proche is often used even for distant future events; futur simple is more common in writing and formal speech.

tables.caption_tr: Common Time Expressions Used with Futur Simple
rows: dans deux jours / dans un an
in two days / in a year

examples.target: Je parlerai français couramment dans un an.
examples.translation_tr: I will speak French fluently in a year.

examples.target: Nous finirons ce projet avant vendredi.
examples.translation_tr: We will finish this project before Friday.

examples.target: Elle vendra sa voiture le mois prochain.
examples.translation_tr: She will sell her car next month.

examples.target: Quand tu arriveras, appelle-moi.
examples.translation_tr: When you arrive, call me.
examples.note_tr: After 'quand' (when) referring to a future event, French uses futur simple in BOTH clauses; English uses present tense in the 'when' clause. This is a very common learner error.

examples.target: S'il pleut demain, nous resterons à la maison.
examples.translation_tr: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
examples.note_tr: With 'si' (if) expressing a real future condition, the si-clause stays in the PRESENT tense; only the main (result) clause takes futur simple. Never put futur simple right after 'si' in this construction.

examples.target: Ils seront très heureux de te voir.
examples.translation_tr: They will be very happy to see you.

examples.target: Je te promets que je ferai de mon mieux.
examples.translation_tr: I promise you that I will do my best.

examples.target: On verra bien ce qui se passera.
examples.translation_tr: We'll see what happens.

modal-verbs.intro_tr: Pouvoir, devoir, vouloir, and savoir are the four core modal verbs of French: they pair with an infinitive to express ability/permission, obligation/probability, desire, and knowledge/skill respectively. All four are highly irregular in the present tense, sharing a pattern where the singular forms (je/tu/il) use one stem, nous/vous use another, and ils/elles return to the singular-type stem with -ent. Their irregularity continues into the futur simple, conditionnel, and subjonctif présent, each with its own unique stem. What makes these verbs especially tricky for English speakers is that their meaning can shift depending on tense and mood; most notably devoir, which can mean "must," "probably," or "owe"; and that pouvoir and savoir both translate as "can" in English but are never interchangeable.

tables.caption_tr: Present Tense Conjugation of pouvoir, devoir, vouloir, savoir
footnotes_tr: Note the stem-change pattern: singular forms use one stem (peu-/doi-/veu-/sai-), nous/vous keep a different stem (pouv-/dev-/voul-/sav-), and ils/elles return to the singular-type stem plus -ent.
In inverted questions with 'je', pouvoir uses the special form 'puis-je ?' instead of 'peux-je' (e.g. Puis-je vous aider ?).

tables.caption_tr: Key Irregular Forms in Other Tenses
footnotes_tr: The circumflex on 'dû' appears only in the masculine singular, to distinguish it from the partitive article 'du'; the feminine and plural forms (due, dus, dues) carry no accent.
All four verbs form the passé composé with avoir: j'ai pu, j'ai dû, j'ai voulu, j'ai su.
Futur simple and conditionnel présent share the same irregular stem, just with different endings: je pourrai / je pourrais, je devrai / je devrais, je voudrai / je voudrais, je saurai / je saurais.

tables.caption_tr: Core Meanings and Typical Constructions
rows: Je peux venir demain. (I can come tomorrow.)
obligation ('must/have to'); probability ('must be'); debt ('to owe')
Tu dois partir. / Il doit être malade. / Je te dois 10 euros.
desire, wish, willingness; polite request in conditionnel
Elle veut partir. (She wants to leave.)
learned skill or knowledge ('know how to'); factual knowledge
Il sait nager. (He knows how to swim.)

tables.caption_tr: Devoir: How Meaning Changes with Tense and Mood
rows: Je devais l'appeler, mais j'ai oublié.
I was supposed to call him, but I forgot.
I had to leave early (and did).
regret or reproach about the past ('should have')
Tu aurais dû me le dire.
footnotes_tr: This tense-based meaning shift is a common exam and comprehension trap; pay close attention to which tense of devoir is used.

tables.caption_tr: Savoir vs. Pouvoir: Two Ways to Say 'Can'
rows: I know how to drive (I learned the skill).
Physical ability or circumstance right now
I can drive tonight (I'm physically/circumstantially able).
May I go out? (asking permission, not skill)
footnotes_tr: A useful test: if you could replace the meaning with 'know how to', use savoir; if it's about being allowed or physically able, use pouvoir.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Modal Verbs
rows: Using 'vouloir dire' literally as 'want to say'
'vouloir dire' is a fixed idiom meaning 'to mean'
Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ? = What does that mean?
Confusing 'je veux' with 'je voudrais' in polite requests
'je veux' sounds blunt or demanding; the conditionnel softens the request
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. (not: Je veux un café)
Adding a circumflex to every form of 'dû'
The circumflex appears only on the masculine singular past participle
dû (m.sg.) but due, dus, dues (no accent)
Using 'pouvoir' for a learned skill like a language
Je sais parler français. (not: Je peux parler français, unless referring to one specific occasion)
Mixing up imparfait vs passé composé of devoir
Imparfait = ongoing/unfulfilled obligation; passé composé = a completed one-time obligation
Je devais venir (but didn't) vs J'ai dû venir (and did)

examples.target: Je peux vous aider si vous voulez.
examples.translation_tr: I can help you if you want.
examples.note_tr: pouvoir = physical/circumstantial ability

examples.target: Tu dois faire tes devoirs avant de sortir.
examples.translation_tr: You must do your homework before going out.
examples.note_tr: devoir + infinitive = obligation

examples.target: Elle veut apprendre le français cette année.
examples.translation_tr: She wants to learn French this year.
examples.note_tr: vouloir = desire/wish

examples.target: Nous savons parler espagnol, mais pas italien.
examples.translation_tr: We know how to speak Spanish, but not Italian.
examples.note_tr: savoir = learned skill

examples.target: Il doit être fatigué après ce long voyage.
examples.translation_tr: He must be tired after that long trip.
examples.note_tr: devoir = probability, not obligation here

examples.target: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.translation_tr: I would like a coffee, please.
examples.note_tr: voudrais (conditionnel) = polite request, softer than 'je veux'

examples.target: Vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici sans badge.
examples.translation_tr: You cannot enter here without a badge.
examples.note_tr: pouvoir + ne...pas = permission denied

examples.target: J'ai dû partir tôt hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: I had to leave early last night.
examples.note_tr: passé composé of devoir = a completed, one-time obligation

object-pronouns.intro_tr: French object pronouns replace a noun that has already been mentioned so you don't repeat it. Direct object pronouns (me, te, le/la, nous, vous, les) replace a noun with no preposition (COD), while indirect object pronouns (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur) replace a noun introduced by "à" and referring to a person (COI). Both types normally stand directly before the conjugated verb (or before the infinitive when there is one), except in the affirmative imperative, where they follow the verb attached by a hyphen. In the passé composé and other compound tenses, a preceding direct object pronoun forces the past participle to agree in gender and number; indirect object pronouns never trigger this agreement.

tables.caption_tr: Direct Object Pronouns (COD); replace a noun with no preposition
rows: Il me voit.; He sees me.
Il te voit.; He sees you.
Il le voit.; He sees him/it.
Il la voit.; He sees her/it.
Il nous voit.; He sees us.
Il vous voit.; He sees you.
Il les voit.; He sees them.
footnotes_tr: le, la become l' before a vowel or mute h: je l'aime, je l'habitue.

tables.caption_tr: Indirect Object Pronouns (COI); replace 'à + person'
rows: Il me parle.; He speaks to me.
Il te parle.; He speaks to you.
Il lui parle.; He speaks to him/her.
Il nous parle.; He speaks to us.
Il vous parle.; He speaks to you.
Il leur parle.; He speaks to them.
footnotes_tr: me, te, nous, vous are identical in the direct and indirect forms; only the 3rd person differs (le/la/les vs lui/leur).

tables.caption_tr: Direct vs. Indirect: How to Tell Which Pronoun to Use
rows: Je regarde Paul. → Je le regarde.
J'attends mes amis. → Je les attends.
Je connais Anne. → Je la connais.
Je téléphone à Paul. → Je lui téléphone.
Je parle à mes parents. → Je leur parle.
Je réponds à ma sœur. → Je lui réponds.
Il ressemble à son père. → Il lui ressemble.
footnotes_tr: A quick test: if you can insert 'to' before the person in English (call TO him = téléphoner à), it is indirect (lui/leur); if not, it is direct (le/la/les).

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Rules by Sentence Type
rows: Je le vois.; I see him.
Je ne le vois pas.; I don't see him.
Je vais le voir. / Je peux lui parler.
Je l'ai vu.; I saw him.
Ne le regarde pas !; Don't look at it/him!
footnotes_tr: In the affirmative imperative only, me/te change to the stressed forms moi/toi after the hyphen.

tables.caption_tr: Past Participle Agreement with Preceding Direct Object
rows: No visible change; already masculine singular.
Les fleurs ? Je les ai achetées.
Je lui ai téléphoné. / Je leur ai parlé.
No agreement; indirect object pronouns never trigger participle agreement.
footnotes_tr: This agreement rule applies only to a preceding DIRECT object (le/la/les, or que in relative clauses), never to lui/leur.

examples.target: Je regarde le film. → Je le regarde.
examples.translation_tr: I'm watching the movie. → I'm watching it.

examples.target: Tu aimes cette chanson ?; Oui, je l'aime beaucoup.
examples.translation_tr: Do you like this song?; Yes, I like it a lot.

examples.target: Il téléphone à sa mère. → Il lui téléphone.
examples.translation_tr: He is calling his mother. → He is calling her.

examples.target: Nous parlons aux enfants. → Nous leur parlons.
examples.translation_tr: We are talking to the children. → We are talking to them.

examples.target: Ne le regarde pas !
examples.translation_tr: Don't look at him/it!

examples.target: Donne-moi ce livre, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation_tr: Give me that book, please.

examples.target: J'ai vu Marie hier ; je l'ai vue au marché.
examples.translation_tr: I saw Marie yesterday; I saw her at the market.

examples.target: Je vais leur écrire une lettre demain.
examples.translation_tr: I am going to write them a letter tomorrow.

y-en-pronouns.intro_tr: The pronouns y and en are two small but essential invariable pronouns used to avoid repeating a noun phrase that was already mentioned or is understood from context. Y usually replaces à (or dans, sur, chez, en) + a place or a thing; never a person. En usually replaces de + a noun, a partitive article (du/de la/des/de l'), a number or quantity expression, or de + a place of origin. Both pronouns are placed directly in front of the verb they depend on (the conjugated verb, or the infinitive if there is one), and they follow a strict order when combined with other object pronouns. Because expressions like 'il y a', 'j'y vais', 'il y en a', and 'je m'en souviens' are everywhere in everyday French, mastering y and en is essential for sounding natural.

tables.caption_tr: Uses of Y (place, and à + thing)
rows: à / dans / sur / chez / en + place
à + a thing or idea (not a person)
Il réussit à finir le travail.

tables.caption_tr: Uses of EN (de + noun, partitive, quantity)
rows: de + a thing (not usually a person)
du / de la / de l' + noun
Indefinite article un/une (in negative or emphatic contexts)

tables.caption_tr: Position of Y and EN in the Sentence
rows: pronoun immediately before the conjugated verb
Je n'y vais pas. / Je n'en mange pas.
J'y suis allé(e). / J'en ai mangé.
pronoun goes right before the infinitive it belongs to
Je vais y aller. / Je veux en manger.
verb-pronoun, joined with a hyphen; -er verbs (tu-form) add -s before y/en
Ne + pronoun + verb (tu-form, no extra -s) + pas
N'y va pas ! / N'en mange pas !

tables.caption_tr: Word Order When Combined With Other Object Pronouns
footnotes_tr: All pronouns in this fixed order are placed before the conjugated verb (or before the infinitive) in affirmative and negative statements.
Example combining slots: Il m'en donne. (me + en) / Je le lui donne. (le + lui) / Elle nous y emmène. (nous + y) / Il y en a. (y + en, a special fixed pair meaning 'there is/are some').

tables.caption_tr: Fixed and Idiomatic Expressions With Y / EN
rows: Il y a deux ans, j'ai déménagé. (Two years ago, I moved.)
Il y en a beaucoup dans le frigo.
to be fed up / to have had enough

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: Choosing Between Y, EN, LE/LA/LES and Disjunctive Pronouns
rows: Je vais à l'école. → J'y vais. (not 'Je la vais')
Je pense à mon frère. → Je pense à lui. (not 'J'y pense', since it's a person)
Je me souviens de ce film. → Je m'en souviens.
Je parle de mon professeur. → Je parle de lui. (standard style prefers the disjunctive pronoun for people)
Direct object noun with no preposition
Je vois mon ami. → Je le vois. (not 'J'en vois' or 'J'y vois')

examples.target: J'y vais tout de suite.
examples.translation_tr: I'm going there right away.
examples.note_tr: y replaces à + place (here, 'to that place')

examples.target: Il y a trois livres sur la table.
examples.translation_tr: There are three books on the table.
examples.note_tr: Fixed expression 'il y a' = 'there is/are'

examples.target: Tu en veux encore ?
examples.translation_tr: Do you want some more (of it)?
examples.note_tr: en replaces a partitive noun already mentioned

examples.target: Nous n'y pensons jamais.
examples.translation_tr: We never think about it.
examples.note_tr: y replaces à + thing/idea; pronoun stays right before the verb even in negation

examples.target: Elle en revient demain.
examples.translation_tr: She is coming back from there tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: en replaces de + place (origin)

examples.target: Vas-y, dépêche-toi !
examples.translation_tr: Go on, hurry up!
examples.note_tr: The tu-imperative of -er verbs adds -s before y/en for pronunciation: va → vas-y

examples.target: Il y en a beaucoup dans le jardin.
examples.translation_tr: There are a lot of them in the garden.
examples.note_tr: y and en can appear together: 'il y en a' = 'there is/are some'

examples.target: Je m'en souviens très bien.
examples.translation_tr: I remember it very well.
examples.note_tr: se souvenir de + noun → s'en souvenir; en replaces the 'de + noun' part

demonstratives.title_tr: Demonstrative Adjectives and Pronouns (ce, cette, celui)
demonstratives.intro_tr: Demonstratives in French point to specific people or things; either as adjectives placed before a noun ("this/that book") or as pronouns that replace a noun entirely ("this one/that one"). The adjective forms (ce, cet, cette, ces) must agree in gender and number with the noun they introduce, with a special masculine form 'cet' used before a vowel sound to ease pronunciation. The pronoun forms (celui, celle, ceux, celles) can never stand alone; they must be followed by -ci/-là, a relative clause (qui/que/dont), or 'de' + noun. Separately, the neuter/invariable forms ceci, cela, ça, and c' refer to ideas, situations, or unnamed things rather than a specific noun, and differ mainly in formality. Mastering this system is essential for avoiding repetition and for contrasting or pointing precisely to things in speech and writing.

tables.caption_tr: Demonstrative Adjectives; 'this/that' before a noun (agreement table)
footnotes_tr: French 'ce/cet/cette/ces' translate BOTH 'this' and 'that'; French does not distinguish proximity in the adjective form alone; add -ci/-là to the noun to specify.
'cet' is often confused with the feminine 'cette' because of the final -t sound, but 'cet' is strictly masculine (used only before vowel/mute h).

tables.caption_tr: Demonstrative Pronouns; full paradigm of 'celui / celle / ceux / celles'
footnotes_tr: These forms can NEVER stand alone (unlike English 'this one'); they must always be followed by -ci/-là, 'de' + noun, or a relative clause (qui/que/dont).

tables.caption_tr: Adding -ci (nearer) and -là (farther) for location or contrast
rows: I prefer this one to that one.
this one (f., near) / that one (f., far)
footnotes_tr: -ci/-là is also used to distinguish 'the former' (celui-là, the one mentioned first/farther) from 'the latter' (celui-ci, the one mentioned last/nearer) in formal writing.
In everyday spoken French, -là is far more common than -ci; -ci is often reserved for explicit contrast.

tables.caption_tr: Neuter (invariable) Demonstratives: ceci, cela, ça, c'
rows: refers to something about to be said, or something physically near
refers to an idea, situation, or something already mentioned
everyday contraction of 'cela'; used constantly in speech
used before any form of 'être' for identification/definition, replacing 'ce/cela'
footnotes_tr: 'cela' is rarely used in casual conversation; native speakers almost always say 'ça' instead.
Never say 'ça est'; always contract to 'c'est' before 'être'.

tables.caption_tr: Celui/Celle/Ceux/Celles + de / qui / que / dont; required completions
rows: sa voiture et celle de son voisin
his/her car and his neighbor's (the one of his neighbor)
celui qui arrive en premier gagne
the one who arrives first wins
footnotes_tr: These pronouns behave exactly like a noun they replace: they must still agree in gender and number with what they stand for.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes & Quick Reference
rows: 'cet' is required before a masculine vowel/mute-h sound.
Je veux celui-ci. / celui que tu as.
'celui' etc. always need -ci/-là, 'de', or a relative clause.
Confusing ça vs cela in formal writing
'ça' is too informal for formal/written register; use 'cela'.
The pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces (maison = feminine), not with the possessor's gender.

examples.target: Ce livre est intéressant.
examples.translation_tr: This book is interesting.
examples.note_tr: 'ce' is used because 'livre' is masculine singular and starts with a consonant sound.

examples.target: Cet homme parle très vite.
examples.translation_tr: This man speaks very fast.
examples.note_tr: 'cet' (not 'ce') is used because 'homme' is masculine singular but starts with a vowel sound.

examples.target: Cette voiture coûte trop cher.
examples.translation_tr: This car costs too much.

examples.target: Ces enfants sont très polis.
examples.translation_tr: These children are very polite.

examples.target: J'aime cette robe-ci, pas cette robe-là.
examples.translation_tr: I like this dress (here), not that dress (there).
examples.note_tr: -ci marks the nearer option, -là the farther one, used to contrast two things.

examples.target: Ma voiture est rouge; celle de mon frère est bleue.
examples.translation_tr: My car is red; my brother's (the one of my brother) is blue.
examples.note_tr: 'celle' replaces 'voiture' (feminine) to avoid repeating the noun; 'celle de' = 'the one belonging to'.

examples.target: Prends celui qui te plaît le plus.
examples.translation_tr: Take the one that you like the most.
examples.note_tr: 'celui qui' introduces a relative clause where the pronoun is the subject.

examples.target: Ça ne me regarde pas, mais cela mérite réflexion.
examples.translation_tr: That's none of my business, but that deserves some thought.
examples.note_tr: 'ça' is the informal spoken form of 'cela'; both are neuter pronouns referring to an idea, not a specific noun.

comparatives.title_tr: Comparison and Superlative (plus... que, le plus)
comparatives.intro_tr: French expresses comparison with three simple markers; plus (more), moins (less), and aussi/autant (as); combined with que (than/as) to compare people, things, or actions. The exact formula changes depending on whether you are comparing an adjective/adverb, a noun (quantity), or a verb (action). The superlative simply adds a definite article (le/la/les) in front of the comparative form to say "the most/least." A handful of very common adjectives and adverbs (bon, bien, mauvais, petit) have irregular comparative and superlative forms that must be memorized separately, since French does not use "plus bon" or "plus bien." Word order, gender/number agreement, and the choice between "de" and "que" are the trickiest parts for beginners.

tables.caption_tr: Comparative structures: three patterns depending on what you compare
rows: Elle est plus grande que moi. / Il court moins vite que toi.
J'ai plus de livres que toi.
footnotes_tr: 'plus' is pronounced [ply] before a consonant, [plyz] (liaison) before a vowel, and [plys] when used alone at the end of a sentence.
With nouns, always use 'de' (not 'que') to attach the noun: 'plus de temps', never 'plus temps'.
'que' introduces the second term of comparison and can be followed by a stressed pronoun: 'plus grand que moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles'.
