It's still a bit odd, all the same.
in a moment / a moment ago (context-dependent)
In any case, thank you very much.
Je ne suis pas du tout fatigué.
Il n'a rien du tout compris.
Il se plaint tout le temps.
Tout compte fait, c'était une bonne idée.
All things considered, it was a good idea.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 'les jours' is masculine plural, so the adjective must be 'tous', not the invariable 'tout'.
'le monde' is grammatically masculine here, so it takes 'tout', not 'toute'.
As an adverb, tout must agree to 'toute' before a feminine adjective beginning with a consonant.
listen to context, not just spelling
'tous les invités' (adjective, -s silent) vs 'Ils sont tous invités' (pronoun, -s pronounced /tus/).
'both' is 'tous les deux' (masc.) or 'toutes les deux' (fem.), always agreeing, never invariable 'tout'.

examples.target: Tout le monde est là.
examples.translation_tr: Everybody is here.
examples.note_tr: tout le monde (= everybody) is always treated as masculine singular, even though it refers to a group.

examples.target: Elle a mangé tout le gâteau.
examples.translation_tr: She ate the whole cake.
examples.note_tr: tout + le/la + noun = 'the whole'.

examples.target: Tous les enfants jouent dehors.
examples.translation_tr: All the children are playing outside.
examples.note_tr: tous les + plural noun = 'all the / every'. Here the final -s of 'tous' is silent.

examples.target: Toutes les filles sont venues.
examples.translation_tr: All the girls came.
examples.note_tr: Feminine plural agreement: toutes les + noun.

connectors-basic.title_tr: Connectors: parce que, donc, pourtant, alors que
connectors-basic.intro_tr: French connectors link ideas of cause, consequence, and contrast, and each of the four words here has its own grammatical behavior. "Parce que" answers the question "pourquoi?" and introduces a dependent clause explaining a reason. "Donc" signals the result of what was just said and joins two independent clauses. "Pourtant" marks a surprising contrast between two facts, while "alors que" introduces a dependent clause that either contrasts two situations or shows two actions happening at the same time. Getting these right matters because French distinguishes carefully between connectors that can start a sentence, connectors that require a comma, and connectors that are followed by a full independent clause versus a subordinate one.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Four Core Connectors
rows: expresses contrast between two situations, or simultaneous actions
footnotes_tr: Subordinating connectors can begin the sentence (with the main clause following); coordinating connectors sit between two clauses that could each stand alone.

tables.caption_tr: Expressing Cause: parce que vs car vs puisque vs comme
rows: neutral, the most common way to give a reason
can start the sentence or appear mid-sentence
Il est resté à la maison parce qu'il était malade.
more formal/written; states an additional fact, close to 'for'
cannot start a sentence; always mid-sentence after a comma
Il est resté à la maison, car il était malade.
the reason is already known or obvious to the listener
can start the sentence or appear mid-sentence
presents the cause first, for emphasis
Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés chez nous.

tables.caption_tr: Expressing Consequence: donc vs alors vs par conséquent vs c'est pourquoi
rows: neutral, very common in speech and writing
usually mid-sentence; can be sentence-initial for emphasis ('Je pense, donc je suis.')
Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
Il pleut, alors je prends un parapluie.
sentence-initial or mid-sentence, followed by a comma
Il pleuvait ; par conséquent, nous sommes restés chez nous.
Il était malade. C'est pourquoi il est resté chez lui.

tables.caption_tr: Expressing Contrast: pourtant vs alors que vs mais vs cependant vs tandis que
rows: 'yet'; a strong, almost surprising contrast within one flow of thought
Elle est petite, pourtant elle joue très bien au basket.
'whereas/while'; contrasts two parallel situations; can also mean simultaneous action
Il aime le café, alors que sa sœur préfère le thé.
simple, everyday contrast, the most basic option
Il est riche, mais il n'est pas heureux.
Il a beaucoup travaillé ; cependant, il a échoué.
close synonym of 'alors que', slightly more literary

rows: yes, especially to emphasize the reason or answer 'pourquoi?'
no comma needed before it mid-sentence
yes, but less common; usually appears mid-sentence
comma before donc when joining two clauses
yes, very common at the start of a sentence
comma often precedes or follows it

footnotes_tr: None of these four connectors trigger the subjunctive; that is reserved for concessive connectors like 'bien que' and 'quoique'.

'parce que' is always followed by the indicative, never the subjunctive

depuis-pendant-il-y-a.title_tr: Time Expressions: depuis, pendant, il y a, dans
depuis-pendant-il-y-a.intro_tr: Depuis, pendant, il y a, and dans are four short words that all translate loosely to English time expressions, but they are NOT interchangeable; each one forces a specific tense and points the sentence in a specific time direction. Depuis links an action that started in the past to the present moment ("since/for"), and famously requires the PRESENT tense in French where English uses a perfect tense ("I have lived here since..."). Pendant describes a bounded, complete duration and works with any tense. Il y a means "ago" and looks backward from now, while dans means "in" and looks forward from now; they are mirror opposites. Getting the tense wrong is the single most common English-speaker mistake with these words, so pay close attention to the "Tense Used" columns below.

tables.caption_tr: Core Overview: What Each Word Means and Which Tense It Takes
rows: A closed, bounded block of time

tables.caption_tr: DEPUIS in Detail: Since / For (Action Still Ongoing)
rows: It has been raining for three days.
Since when have you lived in Paris?
Depuis combien de temps apprends-tu le français ?
How long have you been learning French?
Je n'ai pas vu Marie depuis un mois.
I haven't seen Marie for a month.

tables.caption_tr: PENDANT in Detail: During / For (Bounded Duration)
rows: J'ai vécu à Londres pendant deux ans.
I lived in London for two years (finished).
Je fais du sport pendant une heure chaque jour.
I exercise for an hour every day.
Je serai absent pendant trois jours.
I will be away for three days.
Il a téléphoné pendant que je dormais.
He called while I was sleeping.

tables.caption_tr: IL Y A vs DANS: Mirror Opposites (Past "Ago" vs Future "In")
rows: Elle est arrivée il y a une heure.
Il a déménagé il y a cinq ans.
She will arrive in an hour.
On va déménager dans deux semaines.
We're going to move in two weeks.

subjonctif-usage.title_tr: Uses of the Subjunctive (wish, emotion, doubt)
subjonctif-usage.intro_tr: The subjunctive mood (subjonctif) is used in subordinate clauses introduced by "que" whenever the main clause expresses something subjective rather than an objective fact: a wish, an emotion, a doubt, a necessity, a judgment, or a purpose. Unlike the indicative, which states what is real or certain, the subjunctive signals that the speaker is talking about something wanted, feared, doubted, or merely possible. Most triggers require a change of subject between the two clauses (Je veux qu'il parte); when the subject stays the same, French normally switches to an infinitive instead (Je veux partir). Certain conjunctions (bien que, pour que, avant que...) always impose the subjunctive regardless of subject. This page assumes you already know how to conjugate the subjunctive present (see the companion page on subjunctive present formation) and focuses purely on when to use it.

tables.caption_tr: Main Categories That Trigger the Subjunctive
rows: vouloir que, souhaiter que, désirer que, aimer que, préférer que, exiger que, demander que
to want / wish / prefer / demand that
il faut que, il est nécessaire que, il est essentiel que
être content(e)/triste/heureux(se) que, avoir peur que, regretter que, s'étonner que, être surpris(e) que
to be happy / sad / afraid / surprised that
Je suis content que tu sois là.
douter que, ne pas être sûr(e) que, ne pas penser/croire que, il est douteux que
to doubt / not be sure that
il est important/normal/bizarre/juste que, il vaut mieux que
it is important / strange / better that
Il vaut mieux que tu restes.
Je parle lentement pour qu'il comprenne.
il est possible que, il se peut que, il est impossible que
bien que, quoique, à moins que
Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il travaille.

tables.caption_tr: Conjunctions Always Followed by the Subjunctive
rows: Bien qu'elle soit malade, elle vient.
Je te l'explique pour que tu comprennes.
On ira à moins qu'il ne pleuve.
Il est parti sans que je le sache.
de peur que / de crainte que (ne)
Il chuchote de peur qu'on l'entende.
Je viens à condition que tu m'accompagnes.
qui que, quoi que, où que
footnotes_tr: The 'ne' that appears after avant que, à moins que, de peur/crainte que is the ne explétif: it is NOT a negation and is optional in speech, but common in formal writing (see the ne explétif page).

Je ne suis pas sûr qu'il vienne.
Il est peu probable qu'il vienne.
il paraît que / il me semble que
Il paraît qu'il est parti. (fact, indicative)
rare, formal: Il semble qu'il est fatigué.

Not used with the subjunctive, even negated.

Il faut partir. / Il me faut partir.

tables.caption_tr: Quick Decision Guide: Which Mood to Use?
rows: Does the main clause state a fact or certainty (affirmative belief, report, promise)?
Does the main clause express wish, emotion, doubt, necessity, judgment, or purpose?

Is the subject of both clauses the same person?
Is the subject of both clauses different?

subjonctif-passe.intro_tr: The subjonctif passé (past subjunctive) is a compound tense used to express that an action happened BEFORE the action of the main clause, while the whole sentence still requires the subjunctive mood (opinion, emotion, doubt, wish, certain conjunctions, superlatives, etc.). It is built exactly like the passé composé, but the auxiliary verb (avoir or être) is put into the subjonctif présent instead of the indicative present. All the usual passé composé rules still apply: same choice of auxiliary, same past participle agreement with être-verbs and with preceding direct objects, and the same irregular participles. In practice, it lets you say things like "I'm glad you finished" (aies fini) instead of just "I'm glad you finish" (finisses).

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rule: Subjonctif Présent of Auxiliary + Past Participle
rows: Same verb list as passé composé: most verbs use avoir; movement/state verbs (aller, venir, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, retourner + compounds) and all pronominal verbs use être.
aller → soit allé(e)(s); parler → ait parlé
Conjugate avoir or être in the SUBJONCTIF PRÉSENT (not the indicative present).
que j'aie / que je sois (not que j'ai / que je suis)
Identical form to the one used in passé composé, including irregular participles (fait, dit, pris, mis, écrit, vu, su, pu, dû, voulu...).
que tu aies fait, qu'il ait pris
With être-verbs: participle agrees with the subject. With avoir-verbs: participle agrees with a preceding direct object (COD), never with the subject.
qu'elle soit partie; les lettres que j'aie envoyées
footnotes_tr: The trigger word 'que' is included here as a reminder that the subjunctive is almost always introduced by que/qu'.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation; avoir-Verb Example: parler (que j'aie parlé = that I (have) spoke(n))
Full Conjugation; être-Verb Example: aller (que je sois allé(e) = that I (have) went / that I have gone)
footnotes_tr: 'vous' agreement depends on whether it refers to one person or several, exactly as with regular passé composé.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation; Pronominal Verb Example: se lever (que je me sois levé(e) = that I (have) got up)
Sequence of Tenses: Subjonctif Présent vs Subjonctif Passé
rows: Subordinate action happens at the same time or after the main clause
Je suis content qu'il vienne demain. (he is coming; simultaneous/future)
Subordinate action happened BEFORE the main clause (anteriority)
Je suis content qu'il soit venu hier. (he came; earlier action)
Superlative / 'the only one' + subjunctive, action already completed
C'est le seul livre qu'il ait lu cette année.
Doubt/emotion about something that may have already occurred
Je ne pense pas qu'elle ait vu ce film.
footnotes_tr: Unlike the indicative, French subjunctive has no separate 'futur' form; anteriority vs non-anteriority is the only distinction that matters when choosing between présent and passé.

After 'je ne pense pas que' (negative = doubt)

conditionnel-passe.title_tr: Conditionnel Passé & the Unreal Past (si + plus-que-parfait)
conditionnel-passe.intro_tr: The conditionnel passé (past conditional) is used to talk about actions that would have happened under different past circumstances; but didn't. It is built with the conditionnel présent of avoir or être plus a past participle, exactly like other compound tenses. Its most common job is to form the "unreal past" (often called the third conditional): Si + plus-que-parfait... conditionnel passé, describing a hypothetical past condition and its imagined (but unfulfilled) result. It is also used on its own; without any si-clause; to express regret, reproach, or unconfirmed information (very common in journalism). Since it relies on two tenses you must already know well (plus-que-parfait and conditionnel présent), review those first if they feel shaky.

tables.caption_tr: Step 1; The auxiliary: conditionnel présent of avoir and être
footnotes_tr: The conditionnel passé is simply this auxiliary (in conditionnel présent) + a past participle; the same pattern as passé composé, but with a different auxiliary tense.

tables.caption_tr: Step 2; Full conjugation with a past participle (three verb types)
footnotes_tr: With être-verbs (and reflexive verbs), the past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject, just like in passé composé.
With avoir-verbs, the past participle only agrees with a preceding direct object: 'La lettre qu'il aurait écrite...' (the letter he would have written).

tables.caption_tr: The three conditional sentence types compared
rows: If you come (and you might), we'll eat.
Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais.
If I had money (but I don't), I would travel.
Si j'avais eu de l'argent, j'aurais voyagé.
If I had had money (but I didn't, in the past), I would have traveled.
footnotes_tr: This page focuses on the 3rd type: a past condition that was NOT met, and a past result that therefore never happened.
Never use 'si' + conditionnel in French; 'si' is always followed by présent, imparfait, or plus-que-parfait, never by a conditionnel form.

tables.caption_tr: Si + plus-que-parfait... conditionnel passé; clause order is flexible
rows: Si nous avions su, nous serions restés. (If we had known, we would have stayed.)
Nous serions restés si nous avions su. (We would have stayed if we had known.)
Si tu n'avais pas menti, je t'aurais cru. (If you hadn't lied, I would have believed you.)

tables.caption_tr: Frequently needed irregular past participles
rows: j'aurais pu (I would have been able to)
je serais venu(e) (I would have come)

tables.caption_tr: Uses of conditionnel passé beyond 'si' sentences

reports an unverified past fact, softer than passé composé

'si' is never followed by a conditionnel form

examples.target: Selon la presse, le président aurait démissionné hier.

examples.target: J'aurais aimé vous aider, mais je n'étais pas là.

futur-anterieur.intro_tr: The futur antérieur ("future perfect") expresses an action that WILL HAVE been completed before another future action or moment. It is formed with the futur simple of avoir or être plus the past participle, following the exact same auxiliary-choice and agreement rules as the passé composé. Its two main jobs are: (1) marking anteriority inside a future time frame, almost always triggered by time connectors like quand, dès que, une fois que, aussitôt que, and après que when the main clause is in the futur simple; and (2) expressing a supposition or guess about something that has probably already happened (epistemic use, similar to English "must have"). A key trap for English speakers: after quand/dès que/etc., French requires futur antérieur (or futur simple) where English uses a present or present-perfect form; never "will" in the subordinate clause.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: futur simple of avoir/être (the auxiliary) + past participle
footnotes_tr: Choose avoir or être exactly as you would for the passé composé (most verbs take avoir; a fixed list of ~17 verbs of movement/state plus all reflexive verbs take être).

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation example: parler (avoir-group) vs. partir (être-group)
footnotes_tr: With être, the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject, exactly like in the passé composé.

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive verb example: se lever (futur antérieur)
rows: il se sera levé / elle se sera levée
ils se seront levés / elles se seront levées
footnotes_tr: All reflexive (pronominal) verbs use être as the auxiliary; the reflexive pronoun goes right before the auxiliary.

tables.caption_tr: When to use the futur antérieur
rows: One future action finishes before another future action/moment; almost always with a time connector.
Dès que j'aurai mangé, je partirai.
Marks completion by a specific future point in time.
Expresses a guess/probability about something that has likely already happened; often stands alone, no future meaning at all.
Il n'a pas répondu ; il aura oublié son téléphone.
Occasionally used to comment on something already accomplished, viewed from a future vantage point.
Nous aurons tout essayé, au moins.

tables.caption_tr: Time connectors that trigger futur antérieur (in the earlier-action clause) when the main clause is futur simple
rows: Quand elle aura fini, elle nous rejoindra.
Dès que vous aurez signé, envoyez le document.
Aussitôt qu'ils seront arrivés, on commencera.
Une fois que j'aurai payé, je récupérerai la clé.
Après qu'il aura parlé, nous poserons des questions.
footnotes_tr: ENGLISH TRAP: English uses a present or present-perfect tense after these connectors ('when I finish', 'as soon as she has arrived'), never 'will'. French REQUIRES a future tense (futur simple or futur antérieur) in both clauses when the overall meaning is future.

tables.caption_tr: Futur Antérieur vs. Futur Simple vs. Passé Composé; quick contrast
rows: A future action completed BEFORE another future action/moment
J'aurai fini le travail avant ton arrivée.
I will have finished the work before you arrive.
A completed past action (from the speaker's present viewpoint)

tables.caption_tr: Common irregular past participles (needed to build the futur antérieur)
footnotes_tr: The past participle form and agreement rules are identical to those used in the passé composé.

examples.target: Quand j'aurai fini mes devoirs, je sortirai avec mes amis.
examples.translation_tr: When I have finished (will have finished) my homework, I will go out with my friends.
examples.note_tr: French uses futur antérieur after 'quand' when the main clause is future; English typically uses the present perfect here, not 'will have.'

examples.target: Dès que tu seras arrivé(e), appelle-moi.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as you arrive (have arrived), call me.
examples.note_tr: 'être' verb; past participle agrees with the subject: arrivé/arrivée/arrivés/arrivées.

examples.target: Il aura terminé le rapport avant midi.
examples.translation_tr: He will have finished the report before noon.
examples.note_tr: Straightforward future-perfect meaning, same as English.

examples.target: Elle n'est pas venue ; elle aura eu un empêchement.
examples.translation_tr: She didn't come; she must have had something come up.
examples.note_tr: Epistemic use: futur antérieur expresses a guess/supposition about a past event, not a real future.

examples.target: Une fois que nous aurons mangé, nous irons au cinéma.
examples.translation_tr: Once we have eaten, we will go to the movies.
examples.note_tr: 'une fois que' behaves like 'quand'/'dès que' and requires futur antérieur for the prior action.

examples.target: Vous aurez fini ce travail d'ici vendredi.
examples.translation_tr: You will have finished this work by Friday.
examples.note_tr: Used with a deadline expression ('d'ici' + time).

examples.target: Aussitôt qu'ils seront rentrés, ils nous téléphoneront.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as they get home (have gotten home), they will call us.
examples.note_tr: 'rentrer' takes être; agreement with the plural subject 'ils' gives 'rentrés.'

examples.target: À cette heure-ci demain, j'aurai passé mon examen.
examples.translation_tr: By this time tomorrow, I will have taken my exam.
examples.note_tr: Classic future-perfect 'by [future time]' construction.

past-infinitive.intro_tr: The past infinitive (infinitif passé) expresses an action completed before another action, when both actions share the same subject. It is most commonly introduced by the conjunction 'après' ('after'), forming the pattern 'après avoir/être + past participle'. It is built with the infinitive of avoir or être plus the past participle of the main verb, following the exact same auxiliary-choice rules as the passé composé. When être is the auxiliary; including with all reflexive verbs; the past participle must agree in gender and number with the subject. This compact structure is a stylish alternative to a full subordinate clause with 'après que' or 'quand', and is frequently tested at B2 level.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: The être group includes the classic 'DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP' verbs (devenir, revenir, monter, rester, sortir, venir, aller, naître, descendre, entrer, rentrer, tomber, retourner, arriver, mourir, partir) plus their compounds.
For reflexive verbs, the reflexive pronoun (m', t', s', nous, vous, s') always comes directly before 'être', matching the subject.

tables.caption_tr: Agreement Patterns with être in the Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: With avoir as the auxiliary, the past participle normally stays invariable unless a preceding direct object triggers agreement (see advanced participle agreement).

tables.caption_tr: Negative Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: Unlike simple infinitive negation, both 'ne' and 'pas' stay together directly before the auxiliary infinitive: 'ne pas avoir fait', never 'avoir ne pas fait'.

tables.caption_tr: Past Infinitive vs. Related Structures
rows: Après avoir mangé, il est sorti.
Requires the same subject for both actions; shows the first action is completed before the second.
Après qu'il a mangé, il est sorti.
Used when the two actions have different subjects, or in more explicit/formal style.
Avant de manger, il s'est lavé les mains.
Expresses the action that happens before, viewed from the opposite direction.
En mangeant, il regardait la télé.
Expresses two simultaneous actions, not a sequence.
More literary equivalent of 'après avoir mangé', dropping 'après'.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verbs; Quick Reference for the Past Infinitive

examples.target: Après avoir mangé, il est parti.
examples.translation_tr: After eating (having eaten), he left.

examples.target: Après être arrivée à Paris, Marie a appelé ses parents.
examples.translation_tr: After arriving in Paris, Marie called her parents.
examples.note_tr: 'arrivée' agrees with the feminine subject Marie because the auxiliary is être.

examples.target: Après nous être levés tôt, nous avons pris le petit-déjeuner.
examples.translation_tr: After getting up early, we had breakfast.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive past infinitive: 's'être' becomes 'nous être', and the participle agrees with the subject (masculine plural here).

examples.target: Après avoir fini ses devoirs, il a regardé la télévision.
examples.translation_tr: After finishing his homework, he watched television.

examples.target: Merci de m'avoir aidé pendant ce projet.
examples.translation_tr: Thank you for having helped me during this project.

examples.target: Après ne pas avoir dormi de la nuit, elle était épuisée.
examples.translation_tr: Having not slept all night, she was exhausted.
examples.note_tr: Both negation words 'ne' and 'pas' stay together right before the auxiliary infinitive.

examples.target: Après être sortis, ils ont fermé la porte à clé.
examples.translation_tr: After going out, they locked the door.

examples.target: Excusez-moi d'être arrivé en retard à la réunion.
examples.translation_tr: Excuse me for arriving late to the meeting.

participle-clauses.title_tr: Participle Clauses (ayant terminé, une fois parti)
participle-clauses.intro_tr: Participle clauses let you pack a subordinate idea (time, cause, or condition) into a compact phrase built around a participle, without using a conjunction like quand or parce que. French uses three participle shapes for this job: the simple present participle (parlant), the simple past participle used on its own (une fois parti), and the perfect/compound participle (ayant terminé, étant parti) for an action completed before the main clause. The participle can share the subject of the main clause, or it can bring its own subject in an "absolute" construction (le travail terminé, nous sommes partis). This structure is mostly a feature of formal writing and narration, and the trickiest point is choosing ayant vs étant and getting the agreement right.

tables.caption_tr: The three participle forms
footnotes_tr: The 'nous' stem rule: take the nous-form of the present tense, drop -ons, add -ant (nous parlons → parlant; nous finissons → finissant).

tables.caption_tr: Irregular present participles
footnotes_tr: Note the adjectival cousins of some present participles are spelled differently: savoir → sachant (verb) but 'savant' (adjective, learned); différer → différant (verb) but 'différent' (adjective).

tables.caption_tr: Types of participial clauses and their meaning
rows: Voyant qu'il pleuvait, elle prit un parapluie.
Seeing that it was raining, she took an umbrella.
action completed just before the main clause (cause or sequence)
Ayant terminé son travail, il rentra chez lui.
Having finished his work, he went home.
une fois / sitôt / à peine + past participle, main clause
Une fois arrivé, il téléphona à sa mère.
Once he arrived, he called his mother.
Absolute clause with its own subject
noun/pronoun + past or present participle, main clause (no conjunction)
cause or time, subject differs from the main clause
Le travail terminé, nous sommes partis.
The work being finished, we left.
Dinner being over, they went out.

tables.caption_tr: Agreement rules
rows: Les enfants, courant dans le jardin, riaient.
agrees in gender/number like a normal adjective
une eau courante / des enfants obéissants
Past participle in an absolute clause
agrees with the noun it refers to, like an adjective
La porte fermée, il partit. / Les devoirs finis, ils sortirent.
follows normal avoir-agreement rules: no agreement unless a preceding direct object controls it
Ayant fini ses devoirs, elle sortit. / Les leçons qu'il avait apprises, ...
past participle agrees with the subject, like all être-verbs
Étant arrivée en retard, elle s'excusa. (subject = elle, feminine)
footnotes_tr: Choosing ayant vs étant follows the same rule as choosing avoir vs être in the passé composé: être-verbs (aller, arriver, partir, the 'house of être' verbs, and all reflexive verbs) take étant; everything else takes ayant.

tables.caption_tr: Common words introducing a participial clause
rows: Une fois le repas terminé, ils ont débarrassé la table.
À peine sorti, il a commencé à pleuvoir.
Aussitôt arrivé, il a appelé sa femme.
footnotes_tr: 'À peine' at the start of a clause usually triggers subject-verb inversion in the following main clause in formal style: À peine était-il sorti qu'il commença à pleuvoir.

tables.caption_tr: Participle clauses vs. similar-looking structures
column_headers: Same subject as main clause required?
rows: En sortant, il a fermé la porte. (= as/while he went out)
No; can have its own subject (absolute)
Le temps le permettant, nous sortirons. (weather ≠ subject of 'sortirons')
Après avoir mangé, il est parti.
footnotes_tr: Do not confuse the gérondif (always 'en + -ant', same subject) with the bare present participle clause (no 'en', can take its own subject). This is a classic B2 confusion point.

examples.target: Ayant terminé ses devoirs, elle est sortie jouer.
examples.translation_tr: Having finished her homework, she went out to play.
examples.note_tr: Perfect participle (ayant + past participle) shows the action completed before the main clause.

examples.target: Une fois le contrat signé, les travaux ont commencé.
examples.translation_tr: Once the contract was signed, the work began.
examples.note_tr: 'Une fois' + past participle = absolute clause; 'signé' agrees with 'le contrat' (masculine).

examples.target: Étant arrivés en retard, ils se sont excusés auprès du professeur.
examples.translation_tr: Having arrived late, they apologized to the teacher.
examples.note_tr: 'Étant' is used because 'arriver' takes être in the compound past; the participle agrees with the plural subject 'ils'.

examples.target: Le soleil couché, la température a rapidement chuté.
examples.translation_tr: Once the sun had set, the temperature quickly dropped.
examples.note_tr: Absolute construction with its own subject 'le soleil'; no conjunction, no auxiliary; 'étant' is understood.

examples.target: Sitôt le repas fini, les enfants ont couru jouer dehors.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as the meal was finished, the children ran to play outside.
examples.note_tr: 'Sitôt' + past participle expresses immediacy, similar to 'une fois'.

examples.target: Ayant beaucoup voyagé, elle parle plusieurs langues.
examples.translation_tr: Having traveled a lot, she speaks several languages.
examples.note_tr: Cause/reason reading of the perfect participle clause.

examples.target: La réunion terminée, chacun est rentré chez soi.
examples.translation_tr: The meeting being over, everyone went home.
examples.note_tr: Absolute participial clause; 'terminée' agrees with feminine 'réunion'.

examples.target: N'ayant pas reçu de réponse, il a rappelé le lendemain.
examples.translation_tr: Not having received a reply, he called back the next day.
examples.note_tr: Negation wraps around the auxiliary: ne + ayant + pas.

causative-faire.title_tr: The Causative Construction with faire (faire faire, se faire + infinitive)
causative-faire.intro_tr: The causative construction "faire + infinitive" lets a subject cause, arrange for, or force someone else to perform an action, rather than doing it themselves (e.g. "faire réparer" = to have [something] repaired). Word order changes depending on how many participants the sentence has: just an infinitive and a "causee" (the person made to act), just an infinitive and an object, or both an object and a causee together (introduced by à or par). The reflexive variant "se faire + infinitive" shifts the focus onto the subject: it can mean arranging something for oneself ("se faire couper les cheveux" = to get one's hair cut) or, very commonly, experiencing something happen to oneself, often unwillingly, functioning almost like a passive ("se faire voler" = to get robbed). A key grammar trap: the past participle "fait" in this construction is always invariable; it never agrees with a preceding direct object, unlike ordinary avoir-verbs. Object pronouns generally attach directly before the conjugated form of "faire", and when both an object and a causee are pronominalized, the causee becomes an indirect object pronoun (lui/leur).

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Patterns in faire + infinitive (faire faire)
rows: I have the doctor come / I send for the doctor.
Je fais réparer la voiture par un mécanicien. / Il fait lire le livre à son fils.
I'm having the car repaired by a mechanic. / He has his son read the book.
(causee →) COI pronoun + COD pronoun + faire + infinitive
footnotes_tr: When both an object and a causee are present, the causee is usually introduced by à; par is used mainly when it could be confused with the direct object, or for emphasis on the agent (e.g. with a verb that already takes à for its own object).

tables.caption_tr: Conjugating faire in the Causative Frame (example: faire construire une maison; to have a house built)
footnotes_tr: Only "faire" is conjugated for tense and person; the second verb always stays in the infinitive.
In compound tenses, "fait" never agrees with a preceding direct object pronoun; it is fixed and invariable.

tables.caption_tr: Object Pronoun Placement with faire faire
rows: Je le fais venir. (I have him come.)
Je la fais réparer. (I'm having it repaired; la = the car.)
COD pronoun + COI pronoun + faire + infinitive
Je la lui fais réparer. (I have him/her repair it.)
footnotes_tr: In negative and non-imperative sentences, pronouns attach before the conjugated "faire", not before the infinitive.

tables.caption_tr: Meanings and Uses of se faire + infinitive
rows: Elle se fait couper les cheveux.
Passive / experiential; something happens to the subject, often unwillingly
Il s'est fait voler son portefeuille.
He got his wallet stolen (it happened to him).
Undergoing an action performed by a named agent
Elle s'est fait gronder par le prof.
She got scolded by the teacher.
se faire avoir / se faire plaisir / se faire des amis
to get conned / to treat oneself / to make friends.
footnotes_tr: se faire + infinitive is far more common in spoken French than the true passive (être + past participle) for describing something happening to someone.

tables.caption_tr: Past Participle Agreement: The Invariable "fait" Rule
rows: Unlike ordinary avoir-verbs, "fait" never agrees with a preceding direct object, even a feminine or plural one
Je les ai fait venir. (NOT "faites", even though "les" is feminine plural.)
Same invariability applies to se faire
The reflexive form also keeps "fait" unchanged, regardless of the subject's gender/number
Elle s'est fait couper les cheveux. (NOT "faite")
Contrast: laisser (to let) CAN agree in some cases
This is a classic point of confusion; laisser + infinitive follows different, looser agreement rules than faire
Je les ai laissé(s) partir. (agreement optional/debated) vs. Je les ai fait partir. (never agrees)
footnotes_tr: Treat "fait" as frozen/invariable whenever it directly precedes an infinitive in this construction; this is one of the most frequently tested points in French grammar exams.

tables.caption_tr: faire faire vs. se faire vs. rendre; Avoiding Common Confusions
rows: Subject causes/arranges for someone else to do the action
Je fais laver la voiture. (I have the car washed.)
Subject has something done to/for themselves, or something happens to them
Je me fais laver les cheveux. (I get my hair washed.)
Subject causes someone/something to become a certain state (NOT an action; uses an adjective, not an infinitive)
Ça me rend heureux. (That makes me happy.); NOT "ça me fait heureux".
Subject permits/allows an action, without necessarily arranging or causing it
Je laisse mon fils regarder la télé. (I let my son watch TV.)
footnotes_tr: A very common English-speaker error is using "faire" with an adjective to mean 'make someone [adjective]'; French requires "rendre" for that meaning, reserving "faire" for causing an action (infinitive).

examples.target: Je fais réparer ma voiture.
examples.translation_tr: I'm having my car repaired.
examples.note_tr: Object only ("ma voiture"); the mechanic (causee) is left unspecified.

examples.target: Elle fait pleurer son petit frère.
examples.translation_tr: She makes her little brother cry.
examples.note_tr: "pleurer" is intransitive, so "son petit frère" is the direct object of faire.

examples.target: Nous avons fait construire une maison.
examples.translation_tr: We had a house built.
examples.note_tr: "fait" stays invariable; it never agrees with "maison".

examples.target: Il fait faire ses devoirs à son fils.
examples.translation_tr: He makes his son do his homework.
examples.note_tr: Object ("ses devoirs") + causee introduced by à ("à son fils").

examples.target: Je le lui fais lire.
examples.translation_tr: I have him read it.
examples.note_tr: "le" = the book (COD), "lui" = the causee (COI); both pronouns precede "fais".

examples.target: Je me fais couper les cheveux tous les mois.
examples.translation_tr: I get my hair cut every month.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive causative; the subject arranges for the action to be done to/for themselves.

examples.target: Elle s'est fait voler son sac.
examples.translation_tr: She had her bag stolen. / Her bag got stolen on her.
examples.note_tr: Passive/experiential use of se faire; something happens to the subject, usually unwanted.

examples.target: Ils se sont fait avoir.
examples.translation_tr: They got conned / taken for a ride.
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiomatic expression with se faire; "fait" and "avoir" never change form here.

agreement-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Past Participle Agreement (Fronted Direct Object, Reflexive Verbs)
agreement-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic avoir/être rule, French past‑participle agreement gets tricky when the direct object (COD) is placed BEFORE the verb instead of after it; this happens with the relative pronoun que, with object pronouns (le, la, les, m', t', nous, vous), and with question words like quel or combien de. In these cases the participle must agree in gender and number with that fronted direct object, even though the auxiliary is avoir. Reflexive verbs (conjugated with être) follow a special sub‑rule: the reflexive pronoun se/me/te/nous/vous usually acts as the direct object and triggers agreement, UNLESS the verb already has a separate direct object noun after it, or the verb is inherently "indirect" (like se parler, se téléphoner, se nuire). A handful of fixed expressions (se faire + infinitive, se laisser + infinitive) are always invariable, no matter what. This page collects every sub‑case and exception so you never have to guess again.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Agreement Rule with AVOIR: does the participle change?
rows: No agreement, even though there is a COD
Elle a mangé une pomme.; She ate an apple.
Participle AGREES in gender/number with that COD
La pomme qu'elle a mangée.; The apple that she ate.
Indirect object (à + noun) before or after
La lettre qu'elle a écrite à Paul. (COD=lettre agrees; à Paul is indirect, irrelevant)

tables.caption_tr: What Counts as a 'Fronted Direct Object'; Every Trigger
rows: 'que' refers back to 'les livres' (masc. pl.), and stands before 'ai lus' → lus
COD pronouns: le, la, les, m', t', nous, vous
Cette chanson, je l'ai déjà entendue.
'l'' = la chanson (fem. sing.), placed before the verb → entendue
'quelles chaussures' is the fronted COD (fem. pl.) → portées
'combien de photos' = fronted COD (fem. pl.) → prises
lequel / laquelle / lesquels / lesquelles (relative or interrogative)
SPECIAL CASE: 'en' NEVER triggers agreement, even as fronted quantity; stays invariable

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive Verbs; Full Conjugation of SE LAVER (passé composé)
Reflexive Verbs; When the Participle Does NOT Agree
rows: A direct object noun follows the verb
The reflexive pronoun is then an INDIRECT object (to oneself); the real COD comes after → no agreement
Elle s'est lavé les mains. (les mains = COD, comes after → lavé stays invariable)
Inherently indirect reflexive verbs (se + à qqn)
Verbs like se parler, se téléphoner, se sourire, se nuire, se plaire, se mentir, se succéder normally take à → se is indirect object → invariable
Ils se sont téléphoné tous les jours. (téléphoner À qqn)
'compte' is the real COD in this idiom, se is indirect → always invariable
Elle s'est rendu compte de son erreur.
The reflexive pronoun is indirect (demander/dire À soi-même) → invariable
Elle s'est demandé pourquoi il était parti.

tables.caption_tr: Always-Invariable Special Cases (memorize these)
rows: Elle s'est fait couper les cheveux.
'se faire' + infinitive is ALWAYS invariable, no exceptions
Elle s'est laissé tomber sur le lit.
Traditionally invariable in careful/formal French (modern usage sometimes allows agreement, but invariable is the safe rule)
Verbs of measure used without a true COD (courir, coûter, peser, vivre, dormir, marcher)
Les cent mètres qu'il a courus vs. Les efforts que ça a coûté.
Agrees ONLY when used figuratively/transitively (courir un risque); stays invariable when literal measure of distance/time/price/weight
Impersonal verbs (il a plu, il y a eu, il a fallu)
Les orages qu'il y a eu cette semaine.
With impersonal 'il', the real subject is 'il' itself; participle is always invariable regardless of any apparent COD

examples.target: Les fleurs que j'ai achetées sont magnifiques.
examples.translation_tr: The flowers that I bought are magnificent. (COD 'que' = les fleurs, fronted → participle agrees: achetées)

examples.target: Combien de fautes as-tu faites dans cette dictée?
examples.translation_tr: How many mistakes did you make in this dictation? (fronted COD 'combien de fautes' → faites)

examples.target: Quelle robe as-tu choisie pour la soirée?
examples.translation_tr: Which dress did you choose for the party? (fronted COD 'quelle robe' → choisie)

examples.target: Je les ai vus hier au marché.
examples.translation_tr: I saw them yesterday at the market. (COD pronoun 'les' placed before → vus agrees, masc. plural)

examples.target: Elle s'est lavée avant de sortir.
examples.translation_tr: She washed (herself) before going out. (reflexive pronoun 'se' = direct object → lavée agrees)

examples.target: Elle s'est lavé les mains avant de manger.
examples.translation_tr: She washed her hands before eating. (COD 'les mains' comes AFTER the participle, not 'se' → no agreement: lavé)

examples.target: Ils se sont parlé pendant des heures.
examples.translation_tr: They talked to each other for hours. (se parler à qqn = indirect object → participle stays invariable: parlé)

examples.target: Elle s'est laissé mourir de chagrin.
examples.translation_tr: She let herself die of grief. (se laisser + infinitive is always invariable: laissé)

relative-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Relative Clauses (lequel + preposition, ce qui / ce que)
relative-advanced.intro_tr: Advanced relative clauses in French go beyond the basic qui/que/dont/où system. When a preposition other than 'de' governs the relative pronoun and the antecedent is a thing, French uses forms of lequel (auquel, duquel, avec lequel, etc.), which must agree in gender and number with the noun they replace and contract with à and de. When there is no specific antecedent at all; when the relative clause refers to an idea, a whole situation, or an unspecified 'thing' (like English 'what'); French uses the indefinite set ce qui / ce que / ce dont / ce à quoi instead. The choice among these four depends entirely on which preposition (if any) the verb inside the clause requires. Mastering this system means memorizing which verbs take à or de and applying the contraction rules for lequel consistently.

tables.caption_tr: Lequel and Its Contracted Forms with à and de
rows: avec / pour / sans / sur / dans / chez (no contraction)
footnotes_tr: à and de always fuse with lequel, lesquels, and lesquelles (auquel, duquel, auxquels, desquels...) but NEVER with laquelle (à laquelle, de laquelle stay separate).
All other prepositions (avec, pour, sans, sur, dans, chez, pendant, malgré...) simply precede lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles without any contraction.
lequel and its forms mainly replace THING antecedents; for PEOPLE, 'preposition + qui' is generally preferred in everyday French (see next table).

tables.caption_tr: Indefinite Relative Pronouns: ce qui / ce que / ce dont / ce à quoi (No Specific Antecedent)
rows: direct object of the embedded verb
Ce que je veux, c'est la paix.
Ce dont j'ai peur, c'est l'échec.
What I'm afraid of is failure.
Ce à quoi je pense, c'est mon avenir.
What I'm thinking about is my future.
footnotes_tr: These forms are used when there is NO specific noun antecedent; the pronoun stands for an unspecified idea or thing, similar to English 'what' in 'what I need'.
Compare with qui/que/dont, which always refer back to a specific, named noun already mentioned in the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Relative Pronoun Choice for People vs Things After a Preposition
column_headers: After other prepositions (avec, pour, sur, chez...)
rows: ce + preposition + quoi (e.g. ce sur quoi, ce pour quoi)
footnotes_tr: dont is strongly preferred over 'duquel' and 'de qui' whenever 'de' is required, for both people and things, unless clarity demands otherwise (e.g., inside a longer prepositional phrase like 'à côté duquel').
'ce quoi' alone does not exist; 'quoi' always needs a preposition attached (à quoi, de quoi, sur quoi...) when there is no antecedent.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verb + Preposition Combinations That Control Pronoun Choice
footnotes_tr: Always identify the preposition required by the verb FIRST, then decide between the lequel-form (specific antecedent) or the ce-form (no antecedent).

tables.caption_tr: Set Expressions with tout ce qui / tout ce que / tout ce dont
rows: Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or.
Dis-moi tout ce que tu sais.
Prends tout ce dont tu as besoin.
Ce qui compte, c'est la santé.
Ce que je préfère, c'est le calme.
footnotes_tr: The 'ce qui/ce que ..., c'est ...' construction is a very common way to emphasize a topic in spoken and written French, similar to English 'what X is, is Y'.

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors and Corrections
rows: la personne à qui je pense
penser à requires the preposition à before the relative pronoun; que cannot carry a preposition.
*ce que je pense* (meaning 'what I'm thinking about')
Since penser takes à and there is no antecedent, à quoi is obligatory, not que.
avoir besoin de requires dont, which replaces 'de + antecedent'.
*la femme de laquelle je parle* (everyday speech)
dont is the natural, preferred replacement for 'de + person/thing' in most contexts.
quoi never stands alone after ce without a preposition; que is used when there is no preposition.
footnotes_tr: The most frequent learner error is forgetting the preposition a verb requires (e.g., forgetting that penser needs à, or avoir besoin needs de) and defaulting to que in all cases.

examples.target: Voici le stylo avec lequel j'écris.
examples.translation_tr: Here is the pen (that) I write with.
examples.note_tr: avec lequel = 'with which'; the preposition (avec) determines the form of lequel, which agrees with 'le stylo' (masc. sing.).

examples.target: La femme à qui je parle est ma voisine.
examples.translation_tr: The woman I'm talking to is my neighbor.
examples.note_tr: For people after à, 'à qui' is preferred over 'à laquelle' in everyday speech.

examples.target: C'est le projet auquel je pense depuis des semaines.
examples.translation_tr: That's the project I've been thinking about for weeks.
examples.note_tr: penser à + thing → auquel (à + lequel contracts).

examples.target: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe.
examples.translation_tr: I don't understand what is happening.
examples.note_tr: ce qui = subject of the embedded clause, no specific antecedent ('what' = 'the thing that').

examples.target: Dis-moi ce que tu veux.
examples.translation_tr: Tell me what you want.
examples.note_tr: ce que = direct object of 'veux'; becomes ce qu' before a vowel sound.

examples.target: C'est exactement ce dont j'avais besoin.
examples.translation_tr: That's exactly what I needed.
examples.note_tr: avoir besoin de → ce dont, since 'de' is built into the verb.

examples.target: Ce à quoi je m'intéresse, c'est la musique classique.
examples.translation_tr: What I'm interested in is classical music.
examples.note_tr: s'intéresser à + no antecedent → ce à quoi (never 'ce que' here).

examples.target: Les amis chez qui nous dînons habitent à Lyon.
examples.translation_tr: The friends at whose place we're having dinner live in Lyon.
examples.note_tr: chez + qui for people; chez lequel does not exist for people in standard usage.

cleft-sentences.intro_tr: Cleft sentences with "c'est ... qui / que" let a speaker push one piece of information into the spotlight; the same way English uses "It is ... that/who ..." (e.g., "It's Paul who called," not "Paul called"). French splits the sentence into two parts: "c'est" + the emphasized element, followed by "qui" or "que" + the rest of the original sentence. The choice between "qui" and "que" depends purely on the grammatical role the emphasized element plays inside that second clause: "qui" if it is the subject, "que" if it is anything else (object, time, place, manner, reason). Because this structure is built entirely from words already familiar at a basic level (c'est, qui, que), it can be introduced early, but mastering all its uses; verb agreement, tense shifts of "c'est," and prepositional elements; is what makes it a true B2 skill. This page collects every pattern and pitfall in one place for quick reference.

tables.caption_tr: The Basic Formula: choosing qui vs. que
rows: X is the SUBJECT of the following verb
c'est / ce sont + [emphasized subject] + qui + verb + (rest)
C'est Marie qui a téléphoné. (Marie is the one who called.)
X is the OBJECT or any other element (time, place, manner, reason)
c'est / ce sont + [emphasized element] + que + subject + verb + (rest)
C'est ce livre que je préfère. (This book is the one I prefer.)

tables.caption_tr: Emphasizing different sentence elements
rows: C'est Paul qui a cassé le vase.
It's Paul who broke the vase.
C'est ce film que nous avons vu.
It's this film that we saw.
que (preposition stays with the fronted element)
C'est à Paul que je pense.
This is how it must be done.
C'est parce qu'il pleut que nous restons.
It's because it's raining that we're staying.

tables.caption_tr: Tense agreement of "c'est"
rows: Ce sera toi qui gagneras la course.
Ce serait dommage que tu partes maintenant.
Ç'a été une erreur que de partir si tôt. (very formal/literary)

tables.caption_tr: Verb agreement after "qui" with pronoun subjects
rows: C'est moi qui suis en retard.
C'est elle qui chante le mieux.
Ce sont eux qui partent les premiers.

tables.caption_tr: c'est vs. ce sont before a plural element
rows: Ce sont mes parents qui paient.
Common in everyday speech, but avoid in formal writing.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: "Qui" is required because "Paul" is the subject of "a téléphoné."
C'est le livre qui je préfère.
C'est le livre que je préfère.
"Que" is required because "le livre" is the object of "préfère," not its subject.
C'est moi qui est en retard.
C'est moi qui suis en retard.
The verb after "qui" must agree with the emphasized pronoun ("moi" → "suis"), not default to the 3rd person singular.
Ce sont mes amis que sont venus.
Ce sont mes amis qui sont venus.
"Mes amis" is the subject of "sont venus," so "qui" is needed, not "que."
C'est à Paul que je pense.
When the verb requires a preposition (penser à), the preposition must be kept before the emphasized noun, followed by "que."

examples.target: C'est Marie qui a organisé la fête.
examples.translation_tr: It's Marie who organized the party.
examples.note_tr: Marie is the subject of 'a organisé', so 'qui' is used.

examples.target: C'est ce livre que je te recommande.
examples.translation_tr: It's this book that I recommend to you.
examples.note_tr: 'Ce livre' is the object of 'recommande', so 'que' is used.

examples.target: C'est à toi que je parle.
examples.translation_tr: It's you that I'm talking to.
examples.note_tr: The preposition 'à' stays attached to the emphasized element; 'que' still introduces the clause.

examples.target: C'est demain que nous partons en vacances.
examples.translation_tr: It's tomorrow that we're leaving on vacation.
examples.note_tr: Time expressions are emphasized with 'que', not 'qui'.

examples.target: C'était mon père qui conduisait ce soir-là.
examples.translation_tr: It was my father who was driving that night.
examples.note_tr: 'C'est' shifts to 'c'était' to match the past tense of the sentence.

examples.target: Ce sont eux qui ont gagné le match.
examples.translation_tr: It's them who won the match.
examples.note_tr: 'Ce sont' (plural) is used before a plural emphasized subject in careful style.

examples.target: C'est parce qu'il était malade qu'il n'est pas venu.
examples.translation_tr: It's because he was sick that he didn't come.
examples.note_tr: A reason clause introduced by 'parce que' can also be placed in the cleft frame, ending in 'que'.

examples.target: C'est moi qui suis responsable de cette erreur.
examples.translation_tr: I am the one who is responsible for this mistake.
examples.note_tr: The verb after 'qui' agrees with the emphasized pronoun 'moi' (1st person), not with a default 3rd person form.

nominalization.intro_tr: Nominalization is the process of turning a verb (and occasionally an adjective) into a noun by attaching a suffix such as -tion/-sion, -age, -ment, -ance/-ence, or -ure. French relies heavily on these abstract nouns in formal writing, news, and academic texts, often where English would keep using a verb or gerund ("the organization of the event" instead of "organizing the event"). Each suffix has a strongly predictable grammatical gender: -tion, -sion, -ance, -ence, -ure, and -ison are (almost) always feminine, while -age, -ment, and -isme are (almost) always masculine. The suffix also hints at meaning: -age and -ment often describe a process, action, or result, while -tion/-sion nouns are typically more abstract or administrative. Because spelling and stem changes are not always predictable (e.g., vendre → la vente, not "vendition"), the irregular forms below must simply be memorized alongside the regular patterns. Note: the noun-forming -ment (masculine, added to verbs: changer → changement) is a completely different suffix from the adverb-forming -ment (added to adjectives: rapide → rapidement); do not confuse the two.

tables.caption_tr: Quick Reference: Suffix, Gender, and Typical Source
Verbs → -tion / -sion Nouns (always feminine)
Verbs → -age Nouns (almost always masculine)
Verbs → -ment Nouns (almost always masculine)
Other Common Nominal Suffixes: -ance/-ence, -ure, -ison (always feminine)
Irregular / Unpredictable Nominalizations
rows: the noun is identical to the infinitive
the noun is identical to the infinitive

rows: noun -ment attaches to verbs; adverb -ment attaches to adjectives; different rule sets
treating 'information' as always plural like English 'news'
une information = one piece of news; des informations = the news (broadcast)
French 'information' is countable in the singular, unlike English 'news'

examples.target: Le gouvernement a annoncé de nouvelles mesures économiques.
examples.translation_tr: The government announced new economic measures.
examples.note_tr: 'gouvernement' (masc.) is the -ment nominalization of 'gouverner' (to govern).

examples.target: L'organisation de l'événement a pris plusieurs mois.
examples.translation_tr: The organization of the event took several months.
examples.note_tr: 'organisation' (fem.) comes from 'organiser'; note the -tion suffix triggers l' before a vowel.

examples.target: Le développement économique du pays est très rapide.
examples.translation_tr: The country's economic development is very fast.
examples.note_tr: 'développement' (masc.) is built from 'développer' + -ment.

examples.target: Elle a fait beaucoup de progrès grâce à cet apprentissage intensif.
examples.translation_tr: She made a lot of progress thanks to this intensive learning.
examples.note_tr: 'apprentissage' (masc.) is an -age noun from 'apprendre', with doubled 's' for spelling reasons.

examples.target: Le nettoyage de la maison a duré toute la journée.
examples.translation_tr: The cleaning of the house lasted the whole day.
examples.note_tr: 'nettoyage' (masc.) from 'nettoyer'; typical -age pattern for a process/activity.

examples.target: La décision finale sera prise demain matin.
examples.translation_tr: The final decision will be made tomorrow morning.
examples.note_tr: 'décision' (fem.) is an irregular -tion-family noun from 'décider' (d→sion change).

examples.target: Le paiement doit être effectué avant vendredi.
examples.translation_tr: The payment must be made before Friday.
examples.note_tr: 'paiement' (masc.) keeps the 'e' of 'payer' before -ment, unlike most -er verbs.

examples.target: Sa naissance a eu lieu à Paris, en hiver.
examples.translation_tr: His/her birth took place in Paris, in winter.
examples.note_tr: 'naissance' (fem.) is an -ance noun from the irregular verb 'naître'.

discourse-connectors.intro_tr: Discourse connectors (connecteurs logiques / mots de liaison) are words that link sentences and paragraphs to signal logical relationships such as contrast, consequence, addition, or a shift in reasoning. They are the backbone of formal written French: essays, reports, and argumentative texts rely on them constantly, while everyday speech tends to use simpler equivalents (mais, donc, alors). This page focuses on four B2-level connectors that students often confuse: néanmoins and toutefois (formal 'nevertheless/however'), ainsi (formal 'thus/therefore'), and the tricky little word or, which does NOT mean 'or' in English but introduces a new fact or a turning point in an argument or story. Getting the register, position, and punctuation of these words right is what separates intermediate French from polished, essay-level French.

rows: Formal, written; slightly softer than néanmoins
Neutral; common in speech AND writing
on the other hand, in contrast
Formal, written; also means 'like this' in other contexts
All registers; the default everyday word

Formal, written; NOT the English word 'or'

rows: Strongest, most formal 'nevertheless'; concedes a point fully before contradicting it
Sentence-initial (after ; or .) or after the verb
Slightly softer than néanmoins; often introduces a nuance or reservation rather than a full contradiction
Sentence-initial, or mid-sentence set off by commas
Neutral all-purpose 'however'; safest choice in formal writing when unsure
fact 1 ; cependant, fact 2 / Il est, cependant, absent.
More colloquial feel than the others; frequently used in spoken French too; implies surprise at the contradiction
Requires balancing TWO facts (one downside, one upside, or vice versa); cannot open a text alone
Negative point ; en revanche, positive point.

tables.caption_tr: Understanding OR; The Logical and Narrative Connector (Not the English 'or')
rows: Introduces a new fact or second premise that pushes an argument toward its conclusion (classic syllogism structure)
Marks an unexpected turn or new development in a story, similar to 'now' or 'but then' in English storytelling
Signals that the writer is about to introduce a fact that will be challenged or nuanced next
Everyone agrees that X. Or, recent studies show Y.
'or' is also an unrelated masculine noun meaning 'gold'; context (verb, article) tells them apart
une bague en or (a gold ring) vs. Or, il est arrivé (Now, he arrived)

rows: Yes, often set off by two commas
Comma after if initial; commas around if mid-sentence
Yes; mid-sentence triggers inversion in very formal style

tables.caption_tr: Common Confusions and Mistakes to Avoid
rows: donc = neutral/formal logical consequence, usable everywhere; alors = informal, very common in spoken French, slightly weaker logical link
Formal essay: '...donc, il faut...' / Casual speech: 'Alors, on y va ?'
cependant = written/formal default; pourtant = also spoken, often implies surprise at the contrast
Report: 'Cependant, les résultats...' / Conversation: 'Pourtant, il avait promis !'
ainsi alone = 'thus/therefore'; ainsi que = 'as well as / just like' (a comparison, NOT a consequence)
Ainsi, il a réussi. (thus) vs. Paul, ainsi que Marie, est venu. (as well as)

Or, il pleuvait. (Now, it was raining.) vs. une montre en or (a gold watch)

examples.target: Le projet était très ambitieux ; néanmoins, il a été réalisé dans les délais.
examples.translation_tr: The project was very ambitious; nevertheless, it was completed on time.
examples.note_tr: néanmoins = formal written connector, often preceded by a semicolon or period

examples.target: Nous acceptons votre proposition. Toutefois, quelques modifications seront nécessaires.
examples.translation_tr: We accept your proposal. However, a few modifications will be necessary.
examples.note_tr: toutefois usually starts a new sentence, followed by a comma

examples.target: Il a beaucoup travaillé cette année ; ainsi, il a brillamment réussi son examen.
examples.translation_tr: He worked a lot this year; thus, he passed his exam brilliantly.
examples.note_tr: ainsi here shows consequence/result, not the meaning 'like this'

examples.target: Tous les métaux sont conducteurs. Or, le cuivre est un métal. Donc, le cuivre est conducteur.
examples.translation_tr: All metals are conductors. Now, copper is a metal. Therefore, copper is conductive.
examples.note_tr: classic three-step argument (syllogism): premise / 'or' introduces the second premise / donc gives the conclusion

examples.target: Il pensait être seul dans la maison. Or, quelqu'un l'observait depuis la fenêtre.
examples.translation_tr: He thought he was alone in the house. Now, someone was watching him from the window.
examples.note_tr: narrative 'or' marks an unexpected turn in a story, similar to 'now' or 'but then' in English

examples.target: Elle est très douée ; cependant, elle manque encore de confiance en elle.
examples.translation_tr: She is very talented; however, she still lacks self-confidence.
examples.note_tr: cependant is the most neutral/all-purpose contrast connector, usable in both writing and careful speech

examples.target: Le film est un peu trop long ; en revanche, l'histoire est captivante.
examples.translation_tr: The movie is a bit too long; on the other hand, the story is captivating.
examples.note_tr: en revanche pairs two facts of opposite value (one negative, one positive)

examples.target: Cette bague ancienne est en or massif, pas en plaqué or.
examples.translation_tr: This antique ring is made of solid gold, not gold-plated.
examples.note_tr: warning: 'or' here is the unrelated noun meaning 'gold' (masculine), not the logical connector

indefinite-pronouns.intro_tr: Indefinite pronouns replace a noun without identifying a specific person or thing; they express generality, randomness, or distribution ("each one," "whoever," "anyone at all"). This page focuses on three related families: chacun/chacune (distributive "each one"), quiconque (formal "whoever/anyone," used mainly in writing, legal texts, and after comparatives), and the n'importe + question-word series (n'importe qui/quoi/lequel/où/quand/comment), which expresses indifference; "it doesn't matter who/what/which/where/when/how." Register matters a lot here: quiconque sounds formal or literary, n'importe qui is neutral-to-informal, and chacun is fully neutral and extremely common in everyday speech. Agreement rules are minimal (chacun/chacune agrees in gender only, never in number) but frequently misapplied by learners, so the tables below isolate every pattern and common error.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Main Indefinite Pronouns
rows: agrees in gender only; extremely common
agrees with the noun it replaces
l'un... l'autre / les uns... les autres

tables.caption_tr: chacun / chacune; Full Usage Patterns
rows: Chacun des élèves a un cahier.

tables.caption_tr: n'importe + Question Word; Full Paradigm
quiconque; Formal and Literary Uses

equivalent to n'importe qui in negative or comparative contexts
Il est plus compétent que quiconque.
common after plus... que / mieux... que
After sans, sans que, or a negation
Il est parti sans en parler à quiconque.

tables.caption_tr: Choosing the Right Pronoun by Register and Meaning
rows: Elle parle à n'importe qui. / Elle ne parle à quiconque.
Quiconque le connaît sait qu'il est honnête.
Personne n'est venu. / Nul n'est parfait.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Indefinite Pronouns
rows: que is not part of the n'importe series here
the verb stays 3rd person singular even though the meaning feels plural

Tout le monde est là. / Ils sont tous là.
sounds overly formal/stiff in everyday speech
use n'importe qui instead in informal contexts

examples.target: Chacun a le droit de s'exprimer librement.
examples.translation_tr: Everyone has the right to express themselves freely.

examples.target: Chacune des candidates a présenté son projet.
examples.translation_tr: Each of the candidates presented her project.

examples.target: Quiconque viole ce règlement sera sanctionné.
examples.translation_tr: Whoever violates this rule will be sanctioned.

examples.target: Il est plus doué que quiconque dans cette équipe.
examples.translation_tr: He is more talented than anyone in this team.

examples.target: Tu peux inviter n'importe qui à la fête.
examples.translation_tr: You can invite anyone (at all) to the party.

examples.target: Ne dis pas n'importe quoi, réfléchis avant de parler.
examples.translation_tr: Don't just say anything, think before you speak.

examples.target: Prends n'importe lequel de ces livres, ils sont tous excellents.
examples.translation_tr: Take any one of these books, they're all excellent.

examples.target: Pose ta valise n'importe où, ça n'a pas d'importance.
examples.translation_tr: Put your suitcase anywhere, it doesn't matter.

register-tu-vous.title_tr: Registers in French: Everyday (tu) vs Formal (vous)
register-tu-vous.intro_tr: French, like many languages, marks social distance and formality directly in its grammar through two ways of saying "you": tu (informal, singular) and vous (formal and/or plural). Choosing the wrong one is not a minor stylistic slip; it can sound rude, distant, or overly familiar depending on context, so native speakers pay close attention to it. The choice affects not just the pronoun itself but verb conjugation, possessive adjectives are unaffected but reflexive/object pronouns change (te vs vous), imperative forms, and even vocabulary choice (casual slang vs neutral/formal words). This page maps out when to use tu vs vous, how conjugation and pronouns shift between registers, and how vocabulary and set phrases change in informal vs formal French; a system often called "tutoiement" (using tu) vs "vouvoiement" (using vous).

passe-simple.intro_tr: The passé simple ("simple past" or "literary past") is a written-only narrative tense used in novels, fairy tales, historical texts, and formal biographies to report completed, self-contained past actions. It never appears in everyday speech, conversation, texting, or informal writing; there, passé composé takes over the same function. As a learner, your priority is recognition, not production: focus especially on the third-person singular (il/elle) and plural (ils/elles) forms, since almost all narrative prose uses only those two persons. French verbs fall into four ending patterns for the passé simple; the -ai family (regular -er verbs), the -is family (most -ir/-re verbs and many irregulars), the -us family (mostly -oir verbs and some -re verbs), and the small but frequent -ins family (venir, tenir, and their compounds). Many common irregular verbs (faire, être, avoir, voir, prendre, mettre, dire, naître, mourir) must be memorized individually since their stems don't follow the infinitive in an obvious way.

tables.caption_tr: The four passé simple ending patterns (attached to the verb stem)
footnotes_tr: The 3rd person singular (il/elle) and plural (ils/elles) forms are by far the most important to recognize, since almost all literary narration is written in these two persons.
The nous/vous forms are extremely rare in real texts; many learners never need to produce them actively.

Novels, fairy tales, history books, biographies
Completed past action, same meaning as passé simple but usable in speech
Ongoing, habitual, or descriptive background in the past
Descriptions, settings, repeated past actions, both alongside passé simple and passé composé

examples.target: Il naquit à Paris en 1802 et mourut à Paris en 1885.
