examples.target: Elle ouvrit la porte, entra dans la pièce et s'assit.
examples.translation_tr: She opened the door, entered the room, and sat down.

examples.target: Les soldats combattirent avec courage pendant toute la bataille.
examples.translation_tr: The soldiers fought bravely throughout the whole battle.

examples.target: Napoléon devint empereur des Français en 1804.
examples.translation_tr: Napoleon became Emperor of the French in 1804.

examples.target: Ils partirent tôt le matin sans dire un mot.
examples.translation_tr: They left early in the morning without saying a word.

examples.target: La reine mourut quelques années plus tard, laissant le trône vacant.
examples.translation_tr: The queen died a few years later, leaving the throne vacant.

examples.target: Nous fûmes tous surpris par cette nouvelle inattendue.
examples.translation_tr: We were all surprised by this unexpected news.

examples.target: Il fit un pas en avant, puis s'arrêta net.
examples.translation_tr: He took a step forward, then stopped abruptly.

subjonctif-imparfait.title_tr: Imperfect Subjunctive (Subjonctif Imparfait) and Literary Usage
subjonctif-imparfait.intro_tr: The imperfect subjunctive (subjonctif imparfait) is the past-tense counterpart of the subjonctif présent, used when the main clause of a sentence is in a past tense (imparfait, passé simple, plus-que-parfait) or in the conditionnel, following the classical rule of sequence of tenses (concordance des temps). Today it survives almost exclusively in literary, formal, or historical writing; 19th-century novels, legal and administrative prose, and elevated journalism; and only the 3rd person singular form is ever seen in genuinely contemporary formal French (often in fixed expressions like "fût-ce", "ne fût-ce que", "dût-il"). In everyday spoken French, and even in most written French today, the subjonctif présent is used instead, regardless of the tense of the main clause. Recognizing this tense is essential for reading classic literature and formal/legal texts, but you will almost never need to produce it yourself outside of very formal writing. Its formation is built directly on the passé simple stem, which is why the two tenses are often confused by learners.

tables.caption_tr: Formation rule: from the passé simple stem
rows: Take the passé simple, 2nd person singular (tu) form
Add the imperfect subjunctive endings: -sse, -sses, -^t (circumflex + vowel), -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent
vinsse, vinsses, vînt, vinssions, vinssiez, vinssent
The 3rd person singular always carries a circumflex accent on the vowel before the final -t
il vînt, qu'il fût, qu'il eût

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation; regular verbs (parler, finir, vendre)
Full conjugation; key irregular verbs
Classical sequence of tenses (concordance des temps); literary vs. modern usage
rows: Imparfait / Passé simple / Plus-que-parfait / Conditionnel (Il fallait que...)
Subjonctif imparfait (action simultaneous or future relative to main verb)
Any past main verb, but the subordinate action happened before it
Subjonctif plus-que-parfait instead of conditionnel passé (e.g. 'j'eusse voulu' for 'j'aurais voulu')

tables.caption_tr: The circumflex trap: forms easily confused with other tenses
rows: passé simple of être, no accent, no 'que'
Circumflex + preceding 'que' or concessive conjunction signals subjunctive
passé simple of avoir, no accent
passé simple of faire, no accent
Context: appears after que/bien que/pour que, etc.
passé simple of venir, no accent
Circumflex on î is the only visual difference
fixed literary phrase meaning 'even if it were / be it'
Used in expressions like 'ne fût-ce qu'un instant' (if only for a moment)

tables.caption_tr: Register comparison: when you will (and will not) meet this tense
rows: 'Il fallait que je le fasse', never 'fisse'
Fully productive tense in narrative prose
Legal texts, academic French, very formal speeches
e.g. 'qu'il en fût ainsi', 'à quelque prix que ce fût'
Fixed idiomatic expressions surviving in modern French

examples.target: Il fallait que je le fisse tout de suite.
examples.translation_tr: I had to do it right away. (imperfect subjunctive of 'faire'; highly literary; a modern speaker would say 'il fallait que je le fasse')
examples.note_tr: Classic literary sentence; in spoken/modern French the subjonctif présent 'fasse' replaces 'fisse' even after a past main verb.

examples.target: Je voulais qu'elle vînt me voir avant son départ.
examples.translation_tr: I wanted her to come see me before her departure.
examples.note_tr: 'vînt' = imperfect subjunctive of 'venir', 3rd person singular, note the circumflex accent.

examples.target: Bien qu'il fût malade, il continua à travailler.
examples.translation_tr: Although he was ill, he kept working.
examples.note_tr: 'fût' = imperfect subjunctive of 'être'; do not confuse with 'fut' (passé simple, no accent) or the interrogative-inversion form 'fût-il'.

examples.target: On eût dit qu'elle n'avait jamais souffert.
examples.translation_tr: One would have said that she had never suffered.
examples.note_tr: 'eût dit' is the plus-que-parfait du subjonctif used stylistically instead of the conditionnel passé 'aurait dit'; a hallmark of literary register.

examples.target: Elle craignait qu'il ne perdît patience.
examples.translation_tr: She feared that he might lose patience.
examples.note_tr: 'perdît' = imperfect subjunctive of 'perdre'; note the expletive 'ne' after a verb of fear, kept even in this literary register.

examples.target: Quoiqu'elle fût la plus jeune, elle dirigeait l'entreprise avec autorité.
examples.translation_tr: Although she was the youngest, she ran the company with authority.
examples.note_tr: 'fût' again from 'être'; this whole sentence would read 'Quoiqu'elle soit la plus jeune' in everyday modern French.

examples.target: Le professeur exigea que tous les élèves se tussent.
examples.translation_tr: The teacher demanded that all the students fall silent.
examples.note_tr: 'se tussent' = imperfect subjunctive of the reflexive verb 'se taire'; sounds almost comic to modern ears, which is why it is avoided in speech.

examples.target: Si riche qu'il fût devenu, il n'oublia jamais ses origines.
examples.translation_tr: However rich he had become, he never forgot his origins.
examples.note_tr: 'fût devenu' = pluperfect subjunctive (fût + past participle), used after concessive 'si... que' in a literary narrative.

ne-expletif.title_tr: Expletive ne (ne explétif: avant qu'il ne parte)
ne-expletif.intro_tr: The "ne explétif" (expletive ne) is a purely stylistic ne that appears in certain subordinate clauses without carrying any negative meaning; it does NOT mean "not" and is never paired with "pas". It shows up after verbs and expressions of fear, avoidance, and prevention, after certain subordinating conjunctions (avant que, à moins que, de peur que...), and in comparative clauses of inequality (plus/moins... que). It belongs to careful, formal, and literary registers; in spoken French it is very often dropped entirely, and dropping it never changes the meaning. Because it looks identical to negative ne, correctly recognizing "ne explétif" is a classic advanced (C1) reading and writing skill: you must judge from context and the absence of "pas" whether ne is negating anything at all.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Conjunctions that trigger expletive ne (all followed by the subjunctive)
rows: Il est parti avant qu'elle ne le voie.
He left before she saw him.
Nous irons à moins qu'il ne pleuve.
Il chuchote de peur qu'on ne l'entende.
He whispers for fear of being heard.
Elle se tait de crainte qu'on ne se moque d'elle.
She stays silent for fear of being mocked.
Il est sorti sans que je ne m'en aperçoive.
footnotes_tr: With 'sans que', many style guides consider the expletive ne incorrect or redundant because 'sans' is already negative in meaning; best practice in formal writing is to OMIT ne after sans que, though it is still heard in speech.
The expletive ne is always optional after these conjunctions; omitting it is fully correct and very common, especially in spoken French.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Verbs and expressions of fear, avoidance, and prevention (+ que + subjunctive + optional ne)
rows: Je crains qu'il ne soit malade.
I fear he may be sick.
J'ai peur qu'elle ne vienne pas... (real negation with pas)
Il redoute qu'on ne le renvoie.
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: if the subordinate verb expresses the feared/prevented EVENT ITSELF (positive fact), ne is expletive (no 'pas'). If you add 'pas', you negate that event; a genuinely different, opposite meaning.
'Avoir peur que ... ne + subjunctive' (fearing something WILL happen) vs 'avoir peur que ... ne ... pas + subjunctive' (fearing something will NOT happen); compare the example pair above.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Comparative clauses of inequality (plus/moins/autre... que + ne + indicative or conditional)
rows: Il est plus riche que je ne le croyais.
He is richer than I thought.
C'est moins difficile qu'on ne le dit.
It's less difficult than people say.
Le résultat est meilleur qu'on ne l'espérait.
The result is better than we hoped.
La situation est autre qu'elle ne paraît.
The situation is different than it appears.
footnotes_tr: In comparative clauses, the verb after expletive ne is in the INDICATIVE or CONDITIONAL, never the subjunctive; this is a key difference from the conjunction/fear-verb uses in tables 1 and 2.
This comparative ne is purely stylistic/literary; in everyday spoken French it is almost always dropped: 'Il est plus riche que je le croyais.'

tables.caption_tr: 4. Expletive ne vs. real negation ne...pas; how to tell them apart
rows: Subjunctive (after conjunctions/fear verbs) or indicative/conditional (after comparatives)
Depends on the governing verb, same rule as elsewhere
Formal, written, literary; optional and frequently dropped in speech
avant que, à moins que, de peur que, craindre que, plus... que
Any verb you want to negate
footnotes_tr: The single most reliable test: if there is no 'pas' (or another negative word like 'jamais', 'rien', 'personne') accompanying ne, and the verb is after one of the trigger words in tables 1–3, the ne is almost certainly expletive and carries no negative meaning.

examples.target: Partez avant qu'il ne pleuve.
examples.translation_tr: Leave before it rains. (ne here is purely stylistic; the sentence is NOT negative; 'partez' is a positive command)
examples.note_tr: avant que always triggers subjunctive + optional expletive ne

examples.target: Je crains qu'elle ne soit en retard.
examples.translation_tr: I'm afraid she might be late. (still a positive fear, not 'I'm afraid she is NOT late')
examples.note_tr: craindre que + subjunctive + expletive ne (fear that something WILL happen)

examples.target: Je crains qu'elle ne soit pas en retard.
examples.translation_tr: I'm afraid she is NOT late. (this ne...pas IS real negation, unlike the sentence above)
examples.note_tr: compare with previous example; real negation adds 'pas'

examples.target: Évitez qu'il ne découvre la vérité.
examples.translation_tr: Avoid letting him discover the truth.
examples.note_tr: éviter que + subjunctive + expletive ne

examples.target: Elle est plus intelligente que tu ne le penses.
examples.translation_tr: She is smarter than you think.
examples.note_tr: comparative clause: plus... que + expletive ne + indicative (not subjunctive)

examples.target: À moins qu'il ne change d'avis, nous partirons demain.
examples.translation_tr: Unless he changes his mind, we will leave tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: à moins que + subjunctive + expletive ne

examples.target: Il vaut mieux partir avant qu'elle n'arrive.
examples.translation_tr: It's better to leave before she arrives.
examples.note_tr: n' is the elided form of ne before a vowel sound

examples.target: De peur qu'il ne se perde, elle lui a dessiné un plan.
examples.translation_tr: For fear that he might get lost, she drew him a map.
examples.note_tr: de peur que + subjunctive + expletive ne

inversion-styles.title_tr: Inverted Structures and Stylistic Inversion (peut-être est-il...)
inversion-styles.intro_tr: In formal and literary French, certain adverbs and adverbial expressions placed at the very beginning of a sentence trigger a mandatory subject–verb inversion, a phenomenon known as stylistic inversion (inversion stylistique). This is completely different from question inversion: it occurs inside ordinary declarative statements and is a hallmark of elevated written or journalistic register. The most common triggers are peut-être (maybe), sans doute (probably), aussi (so/therefore), à peine (hardly/scarcely), encore (still/yet), ainsi (thus), and du moins (at least). Depending on whether the subject is a pronoun or a noun, you use either simple inversion (verb-pronoun) or complex inversion (noun subject + verb + resumptive pronoun), and a euphonic -t- is inserted between two vowels for pronunciation. In everyday spoken French, native speakers usually avoid the inversion altogether by adding que after the adverb and keeping normal word order.

tables.caption_tr: Adverbs and Expressions That Trigger Stylistic Inversion
rows: Peut-être qu'il est malade. / Il est peut-être malade.
Sans doute qu'elle a raison. / Elle a sans doute raison.
Il pleuvait ; aussi resta-t-il chez lui.
Il pleuvait, donc il est resté chez lui.
À peine était-il arrivé qu'il repartit.
Il était à peine arrivé qu'il repartit.
En vain a-t-il cherché une solution.
Il a cherché en vain une solution.
Tout au plus pourrait-on regretter cela.
On pourrait tout au plus regretter cela.
footnotes_tr: The 'everyday alternative' with que is always acceptable and far more common in speech; the inverted form is reserved for careful writing, journalism, and literature.

tables.caption_tr: Two Types of Stylistic Inversion
rows: The subject is already a pronoun (je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles)
noun subject + verb + hyphen + resumptive pronoun (il/elle/ils/elles)
The subject is a noun or noun phrase
footnotes_tr: In complex inversion the noun subject stays in its normal pre-verb position; only a 'copy' pronoun matching its gender/number is added after the verb.

tables.caption_tr: Full Pronoun Paradigm: peut-être + venir (futur simple)
footnotes_tr: The je-form (viendrai-je) is extremely formal/literary and rare even in writing; speakers typically rephrase with que instead.

tables.caption_tr: The Euphonic -t- Insertion Rule
rows: Verb ends in -e or -a before il / elle / on
Insert -t- between verb and pronoun to avoid a vowel clash
parle → parle-t-il ; a → a-t-il ; ira → ira-t-elle
No extra -t- is added (the -d- is pronounced /t/)
Verb ends in a consonant before je/tu/nous/vous/ils/elles
No -t- is inserted; pronoun attaches directly

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: Literary Inversion vs Everyday French
rows: adverb moved to mid- or end-sentence, normal word order
footnotes_tr: All three sentences mean the same thing; only the register changes. Choose inversion for essays, articles, and literary narration.

tables.caption_tr: Inversion in Incise Clauses (Reported Speech Tags)
rows: « Je pars, dit-il, tout de suite. »
footnotes_tr: Unlike stylistic inversion after adverbs, incise clauses with a noun subject never add a resumptive pronoun: you say 'dit Paul', not 'dit-il Paul'.

examples.target: Peut-être est-il déjà parti.
examples.translation_tr: Maybe he has already left.

examples.target: Sans doute a-t-elle oublié notre rendez-vous.
examples.translation_tr: She has probably forgotten our appointment.

examples.target: À peine était-elle sortie qu'il se mit à pleuvoir.
examples.translation_tr: She had barely gone out when it started to rain.

examples.target: Ainsi parla le vieux sage.
examples.translation_tr: Thus spoke the old sage.

examples.target: Aussi décida-t-il de partir sur-le-champ.
examples.translation_tr: So he decided to leave at once.

examples.target: Encore faudrait-il qu'il accepte.
examples.translation_tr: He would still have to agree to it, though.

examples.target: Du moins peut-on espérer une amélioration.
examples.translation_tr: At least one can hope for an improvement.

examples.target: « Je reviens tout de suite », dit-elle en souriant.
examples.translation_tr: "I'll be right back," she said, smiling.

concession-opposition.title_tr: Concession and Opposition (bien que, quoique, avoir beau)
concession-opposition.intro_tr: Concession and opposition structures let you say that something happens despite an obstacle, or that two facts contrast with each other. French has three main grammatical families for this: subordinating conjunctions like bien que and quoique that require the subjunctive, the fixed idiom avoir beau + infinitive that uses the indicative and needs no subjunctive at all, and prepositions like malgré and en dépit de that are followed directly by a noun rather than a clause. Adverbs such as pourtant, cependant, and quand même (covered in the text-connectors topic) add opposition between two independent sentences instead of linking a subordinate clause. Getting the right construction matched to the right mood (subjunctive vs. indicative) and the right complement (clause, infinitive, or noun) is the main challenge at this level, along with not confusing quoique (although) with quoi que (whatever).

tables.caption_tr: Concessive Conjunctions That Require the Subjunctive
rows: neutral, the most common choice in all registers
Bien qu'il pleuve, elle sort sans parapluie.
neutral to slightly literary; can be followed directly by an adjective
Quoiqu'il soit riche, il est avare.
although / even if you consider that...
formal, used to qualify or nuance a previous statement
Il a raison, encore qu'il exagère un peu.
traditionally considered incorrect except in the fixed phrase 'malgré que j'en aie' (whether I like it or not); avoid in formal writing, prefer bien que
Malgré qu'il pleuve, nous sortons. (avoid in careful French)
literary, often with inversion of the verb and subject
Si difficile que soit l'examen, il le réussira.
literary, synonym of si...que in this use
Pour intelligent qu'il soit, il se trompe parfois.
Qui que vous soyez, vous devez respecter les règles.
formal; two words, not to be confused with quoique
Quoi que tu fasses, reste honnête.
Où que tu ailles, je te suivrai.
formal; 'que' + noun subject + subjunctive of être usually
Quelles que soient les difficultés, il persiste.

tables.caption_tr: avoir beau + Infinitive: 'No Matter How Much...' (No Subjunctive Needed)
rows: Il a beau étudier, il ne comprend rien.
No matter how much he studies, he understands nothing.
Il avait beau crier, personne ne l'entendait.
No matter how much he shouted, no one heard him.
Il a eu beau chercher, il n'a rien trouvé.
No matter how much he searched, he found nothing.
Tu auras beau insister, je ne changerai pas d'avis.
No matter how much you insist, I won't change my mind.

tables.caption_tr: Prepositions and Adverbs of Concession/Opposition (No Subjunctive)
rows: Malgré la fatigue, il a terminé la course.
En dépit de ses efforts, il a échoué.
Sans être expert, il a résolu le problème.
Même si tu as raison, reste calme.
Il pleut ; nous sortons quand même.
Il est malade, pourtant il travaille.

tables.caption_tr: quoique vs. quoi que: Don't Confuse Them
rows: Quoiqu'il soit fatigué, il finit son travail.
Quoi que vous décidiez, je vous soutiendrai.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison Table: Choosing the Right Concession Structure
rows: Do not use with the indicative: NOT 'bien qu'il est fatigué'.
Do not write it as two words unless you mean 'whatever'.
Best avoided in formal writing; use bien que instead.
NOT 'même s'il soit malade'; always indicative after même si.
No subordinate clause, no subjunctive; the infinitive never changes for tense.
Cannot be directly followed by a full clause: NOT 'malgré qu'il pleuve' in careful style; use malgré + noun or bien que + clause.

tables.caption_tr: Ellipsis After bien que / quoique (Same Subject as Main Clause)
rows: Bien que malade, il est venu travailler.
Although sick, he came to work.
Quoique fatiguée, elle a terminé le rapport.
Although tired, she finished the report.
footnotes_tr: This ellipsis is only possible when the subject of the concessive clause is identical to the subject of the main clause.

examples.target: Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il continue à travailler.
examples.translation_tr: Although he is tired, he keeps working.

examples.target: Quoiqu'elle soit jeune, elle dirige déjà son entreprise.
examples.translation_tr: Although she is young, she already runs her company.

examples.target: Il a beau insister, elle ne changera pas d'avis.
examples.translation_tr: No matter how much he insists, she won't change her mind.

examples.target: Malgré la pluie, nous avons fait la randonnée.
examples.translation_tr: Despite the rain, we went hiking.

examples.target: Même si tu as raison, tu dois rester poli.
examples.translation_tr: Even if you're right, you must remain polite.
examples.note_tr: même si is always followed by the indicative, never the subjunctive.

examples.target: Quoi qu'il arrive, je resterai à tes côtés.
examples.translation_tr: Whatever happens, I will stay by your side.
examples.note_tr: quoi que (two words) means 'whatever', not to be confused with quoique (one word) meaning 'although'.

examples.target: Bien que fatiguée, elle a fini son rapport avant minuit.
examples.translation_tr: Although tired, she finished her report before midnight.
examples.note_tr: Elliptical construction: bien que + adjective, verb être omitted since subject is the same as the main clause.

examples.target: Si intelligent qu'il soit, il ne peut pas tout savoir.
examples.translation_tr: However intelligent he may be, he cannot know everything.
examples.note_tr: Literary structure: adjective + que + subjunctive, meaning 'however [adjective] he may be'.

mise-en-relief.title_tr: Fronting and Topic–Comment Structures (quant à, ce que... c'est)
mise-en-relief.intro_tr: Mise en relief ("highlighting") covers the French devices used to move an element out of its normal syntactic slot and place it at the front (or in a special frame) to mark it as the topic of discussion or to give it contrastive emphasis; something English often does with intonation alone, but French does structurally. There are two main families: topic-announcing expressions (quant à, en ce qui concerne, pour ce qui est de) that say "as for X" before the comment, and cleft/pseudo-cleft constructions built around the relative pronouns ce qui / ce que / ce dont plus c'est, or the frame c'est...qui/que, which isolate one constituent for focus. Choosing the right relative pronoun depends entirely on the grammatical function the fronted element would normally have (subject, direct object, or object of "de"). This is a hallmark of formal written and spoken register (C1+), frequent in essays, speeches, and careful conversation. Mastery requires knowing verb agreement (c'est vs ce sont) and how topic markers differ subtly in formality.

tables.caption_tr: Topic-announcing expressions: "as for..." / "regarding..."
rows: Quant à + [topic], + [comment clause, often with resumptive pronoun]
Pour ce qui est de + noun
Pour ce qui est de + [topic], + [comment clause]
footnotes_tr: The topic phrase is normally set off by a comma and often echoed later by a pronoun (elle, il, ça, en, y) that matches its grammatical role in the comment clause.
Quant à contracts with à: quant à + le → no contraction needed since à is fixed before the article (quant au, quant à la, quant aux).

tables.caption_tr: Pseudo-cleft (topic–comment) constructions: ce qui / ce que / ce dont / ce à quoi ... c'est
rows: Ce qui compte, c'est ta santé. (What matters is your health.)
Direct object of the embedded clause
Ce que je veux, c'est partir. (What I want is to leave.)
Object introduced by "de" (parler de, avoir besoin de...)
Ce dont on a besoin, c'est de temps. (What we need is time.)
Object introduced by "à" (penser à, s'attendre à...)
Ce à quoi + [subject + verb + à], c'est + [comment]
Ce à quoi je pense, c'est à notre avenir. (What I'm thinking about is our future.)
Là où je vis, c'est calme. (Where I live is quiet.)
Ce pour quoi / celui qui, etc.
Ce pour quoi il se bat, c'est la justice. (What he fights for is justice.)
footnotes_tr: The comment after c'est can be a noun, an infinitive, an adjective, or a full clause introduced by que.
This structure can also be reversed: C'est + [comment] + que + ce que/ce qui... (rarer, heavier style), e.g. C'est ta santé qui compte, in effect merging with the plain cleft below.

tables.caption_tr: Cleft sentences for contrastive focus: c'est ... qui / que / dont / où
rows: The verb after qui agrees with the focused subject, not with c'est.
C'est ce film que nous avons vu hier.
Que never elides its grammatical role; word order after que returns to normal (subject–verb).
C'est de ce projet dont il parlait.
Some prescriptive grammars prefer c'est de ce projet qu'il parlait (avoiding the dont), both are heard.
C'est ici que tout a commencé.
Où is possible with concrete places: C'est la maison où je suis né.
C'est avec elle que je veux partir.
The preposition stays attached to the focused noun/pronoun, not to que.
footnotes_tr: Cleft sentences highlight exactly one constituent, often implying a contrast ("it's HIM, not someone else, who...").

tables.caption_tr: Agreement and tense in the copula: c'est vs ce sont, tense matching
rows: Focused/commented element is singular or an infinitive/clause
Ce que j'aime, c'est lire. / C'est Paul qui vient.
Focused/commented element is a plural noun (formal register)
Ce sont mes parents qui décident.
Comment clause is in the past
Ce qui l'a surpris, c'était son silence. (Tense of être matches the surrounding narration.)
c'est nous/vous qui + verb agreeing with nous/vous
footnotes_tr: In careful written French, ce sont is preferred before a plural noun; c'est is widely accepted in speech.

tables.caption_tr: Common learner errors
rows: *Ce que je pense, c'est à l'avenir.
"Penser" here needs the preposition à, so ce que (direct object pronoun) is the wrong relative
Ce à quoi je pense, c'est à l'avenir.
*Ce qui j'ai besoin, c'est de vacances.
"Avoir besoin de" requires ce dont, not ce qui
Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de vacances.
The focused element is the subject, so qui is required, not que
Quant à moi, je crois que... (used to open every sentence excessively)
Quant à is a marked, contrastive topic-shifter, not a neutral filler; overusing it sounds unnatural
Use pour moi or je crois que directly in most casual contexts; reserve quant à for genuine contrast.
Verb must agree with the true focused subject (mes amis = plural), not with c'est
Ce sont mes amis qui viennent.

examples.target: Quant à Marie, elle a décidé de rester à Paris.
examples.translation_tr: As for Marie, she decided to stay in Paris.
examples.note_tr: "Quant à" isolates the topic before the comment clause; the topic is often resumed by a pronoun (elle).

examples.target: En ce qui concerne le budget, nous devons attendre la réunion de jeudi.
examples.translation_tr: As for the budget, we have to wait for Thursday's meeting.

examples.target: Ce que je préfère, c'est le silence du matin.
examples.translation_tr: What I prefer is the silence of the morning.
examples.note_tr: "Ce que" replaces a direct object (je préfère quoi → ce que je préfère).

examples.target: Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est la manière dont il a résolu le problème.
examples.translation_tr: What interests me is the way he solved the problem.
examples.note_tr: "Ce qui" replaces a subject (qu'est-ce qui m'intéresse).

examples.target: Ce dont elle a envie, c'est d'un peu de repos.
examples.translation_tr: What she wants is a bit of rest.
examples.note_tr: "Ce dont" is required because "avoir envie de" takes the preposition de.

examples.target: C'est ce livre que je cherchais depuis des semaines.
examples.translation_tr: It's this book that I had been looking for for weeks.
examples.note_tr: Cleft sentence for contrastive focus on the direct object.

examples.target: Pour ce qui est des détails techniques, adressez-vous à l'ingénieur.
examples.translation_tr: Regarding the technical details, please speak to the engineer.

examples.target: Ce sont ces documents-là qu'il faut signer en priorité.
examples.translation_tr: It is those documents that must be signed as a priority.
examples.note_tr: "Ce sont" is used instead of "c'est" because the focused element is plural.

formal-prepositional-phrases.title_tr: Formal Prepositional Phrases (à l'égard de, en dépit de, au sein de)
formal-prepositional-phrases.intro_tr: Formal prepositional phrases such as à l'égard de, en dépit de, and au sein de are multi-word expressions used mainly in written, administrative, legal, journalistic, and academic French to express relations like opposition, cause, context, or benefit with more precision and a higher register than simple prepositions. Almost all of these phrases end in de, so they contract with a following definite article (de + le → du, de + les → des) and some replace de + pronoun with a possessive determiner instead. They are largely interchangeable in meaning with everyday prepositions (malgré, envers, dans, à cause de) but signal formality; useful for essays, reports, news articles, and official documents. This page groups the most common phrases by meaning, explains their exact syntax, and contrasts them with their neutral equivalents so you can both recognize them in texts and reproduce them correctly in your own writing.

tables.caption_tr: Core Formal Prepositional Phrases and Their Meanings
rows: Attitudes, measures, or feelings directed at someone/something; administrative & personal register
Concession; same meaning as malgré but more formal/written
Inside an organization, group, or institution; corporate/academic register
Relation or attitude between two parties; slightly formal but also used in speech
with regard to, in light of
Legal/administrative comparison against a standard or law
Introducing the context/project under which something happens
Introducing a domain or subject area, often policy-related
Legal justification, citing a law, contract, or rule
Introducing a cause/justification, common in reports and formal letters
Neutral-to-formal cause; more written than à cause de

tables.caption_tr: Extended Reference List by Semantic Function
rows: in view of, having regard to
for the benefit of, in favor of
with regard to, in light of
failing that, in the absence of

tables.caption_tr: Syntax: Attaching a Noun, Pronoun, or Clause
rows: Basic pattern: phrase ends in de, followed directly by the noun (with its article).
de + le → du / de + les → des
au sein du gouvernement / en dépit des critiques
Standard contraction rules apply, since de precedes a definite article.
à l'égard de + pronoun → possessive determiner
à son égard, à leur égard, à mon égard
Irregular pattern specific to égard: replace 'de + pronoun' with a possessive (mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur égard).
vis-à-vis de moi, vis-à-vis de lui
Unlike égard, vis-à-vis de keeps de + disjunctive pronoun directly; no possessive substitution.
Phrase + du fait que / de ce que
en dépit du fait qu'il pleuve, compte tenu du fait que...
To introduce a full clause instead of a noun, insert 'du fait que' + indicative or subjunctive as required by the connector.
dans le cadre de + nominalized verb
dans le cadre de la réforme en cours
Works well with nominalizations (-tion, -ment) since the phrase needs a noun, not a verb.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Confusions
rows: malgré la pluie / en dépit de la pluie
Malgré is a simple preposition and takes no de before the noun; en dépit de already contains de, so don't add a second one.
Égard always needs the article l' in this fixed phrase; you cannot drop it.
De + le must contract to du before a masculine noun; au sein de le is never written.
The phrase is vis-à-vis DE (not à) + pronoun; also remember the hyphens: vis-à-vis.
à l'égard de moi / à l'égard de lui
à mon égard / à son égard
With égard, a personal pronoun after de is normally replaced by the matching possessive determiner.
en dépit de tout / malgré tout
Don't combine the two synonyms in one phrase; choose either en dépit de or malgré, not both.

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: Formal Phrase vs. Everyday Equivalent
rows: En dépit de la pluie, il est sorti courir.
Malgré la pluie, il est sorti courir.
Il est très courtois à l'égard de ses invités.
Il est très courtois envers ses invités.
Au sein de l'équipe, chacun a un rôle précis.
Dans l'équipe, chacun a un rôle précis.
En raison du mauvais temps, le vol est annulé.
Le vol est annulé parce qu'il fait mauvais temps.
Par le biais de ce logiciel, on gagne du temps.
Avec ce logiciel, on gagne du temps.
Au moyen d'une échelle, il a atteint le toit.
Avec une échelle, il a atteint le toit.
footnotes_tr: These formal phrases are not 'more correct' than their neutral equivalents; they are simply more typical of written, administrative, or academic registers; using them constantly in casual conversation can sound stilted.

examples.target: Le gouvernement a pris de nouvelles mesures à l'égard des réfugiés.
examples.translation_tr: The government has taken new measures with regard to the refugees.

examples.target: En dépit des difficultés, elle a terminé son projet à temps.
examples.translation_tr: Despite the difficulties, she finished her project on time.

examples.target: Au sein de l'entreprise, la communication entre services reste un défi.
examples.translation_tr: Within the company, communication between departments remains a challenge.

examples.target: Vis-à-vis de ses collègues, il se montre toujours respectueux.
examples.translation_tr: Towards his colleagues, he always behaves respectfully.

examples.target: Cette décision a été prise en vertu de la loi votée en 2015.
examples.translation_tr: This decision was made by virtue of the law passed in 2015.

examples.target: Compte tenu de la situation économique, les prix ont fortement augmenté.
examples.translation_tr: Given the economic situation, prices have risen sharply.

examples.target: Il a agi à l'encontre des règles établies par le règlement intérieur.
examples.translation_tr: He acted against the rules established by the internal regulations.

examples.target: Par le biais de ce programme, de nombreux emplois ont été créés.
examples.translation_tr: Through this program, many jobs have been created.

modalization.title_tr: Modalization and Distancing (sembler, paraître, epistemic devoir)
modalization.intro_tr: In French, modalization (la modalisation) refers to the ways a speaker signals their degree of certainty about a statement, or deliberately distances themselves from full responsibility for it; instead of asserting a fact outright, the speaker frames it as an impression, a rumor, or a calculated probability. The core tools for this are the verbs sembler and paraître ("to seem, to appear") and the epistemic (non-obligation) use of devoir ("must be, must have"), together with expressions like avoir l'air, on dirait que, and il paraît que. Mastering modalization means knowing not only the verb forms but also which mood; indicative or subjunctive; follows each construction, and how to tell epistemic devoir (probability: "he must be tired") apart from deontic devoir (obligation: "he must leave"). This distancing register is a hallmark of advanced, nuanced French, essential for academic writing, journalism, and sophisticated spoken style.

tables.caption_tr: sembler – Full Conjugation (Regular -er Verb)
footnotes_tr: sembler is impersonal-friendly: it is used constantly as 'il semble que...' and 'il me semble que...'; these impersonal forms are the most common uses in advanced French, more common than personal forms like 'tu sembles fatigué'.

tables.caption_tr: paraître – Full Conjugation (Irregular -aître Verb, like connaître)
footnotes_tr: The circumflex accent (î) appears only where the verb stem is directly followed by 't' (il paraît, je paraîtrai, je paraîtrais); this is a very common spelling error to watch for.
Passé composé of paraître uses avoir + paru (invariable past participle).

tables.caption_tr: devoir – Full Conjugation (Used for Epistemic Probability)
footnotes_tr: 'dû' (masculine singular past participle) keeps its circumflex only in the masculine singular form; it is written 'due, dus, dues' without the accent in agreement forms (rare, since devoir mostly takes 'avoir' with an invariable object here).

tables.caption_tr: sembler vs. paraître: Key Differences
rows: subjective impression / personal judgment or inference
objective, often visible or public appearance
opinion, reasoning ('it seems to me that...')
il semble que + subjunctive (or indicative with dative pronoun)
'to be published'; Ce roman paraît en mars. (This novel comes out in March.)
neutral, extremely frequent in speech and writing
slightly more literary/formal, common in written French

tables.caption_tr: Mood Choice After Verbs of Appearance (sembler / paraître)
rows: No mood choice needed; subject of sembler = subject of infinitive.
Expresses genuine doubt or uncertainty about the fact.
Il me semble qu'il est malade.
Adding a dative pronoun personalizes the impression and treats it as near-certain.
Il semble bien qu'il a raison.
Adverbs like 'bien' reduce doubt, favoring the indicative in modern usage.
Il ne semble pas qu'il soit venu.
Negation increases uncertainty, reinforcing the subjunctive.
Reports hearsay/rumor as a stated (if unverified) fact; never subjunctive.

tables.caption_tr: Epistemic devoir: Degrees of Probability (Not Obligation)
rows: Strong logical probability about the present ('he must be').
Strong probability about a past event ('he must have').
Probability within past narration ('he must have been / was probably').
Softer, more tentative probability ('he should be, presumably').
Expectation that an action is already complete ('should have finished by now'); still epistemic.
NOT epistemic; deontic reproach for an unfulfilled obligation ('should have come, but didn't').
footnotes_tr: Telling epistemic (probability) devoir apart from deontic (obligation) devoir depends entirely on context, since the forms are identical: 'Il doit partir' can mean 'He must be leaving (probably)' or 'He has to leave (obligation)'.
'aurait dû' is almost always deontic/regretful in everyday use, unlike the epistemic 'devrait avoir + past participle'.

tables.caption_tr: Other Modalizing / Distancing Expressions
rows: avoir l'air + adjective / avoir l'air de + infinitive
Visible impression; the adjective may agree with the subject (fatiguée) or stay masculine, agreeing with 'air' (fatigué); both are correct.
Sensory/visual impression, very common in spoken French ('it looks/sounds like').
À ce qu'il paraît, il a démissionné.
Formal equivalent of 'apparently, so I've heard'.
Il est censé arriver à midi.
'Supposed to'; expectation based on a plan or rule, with implied doubt about fulfillment.
Selon toute vraisemblance, il a menti.
'In all likelihood'; formal/academic hedging, common in essays and journalism.
'Allegedly'; signals skepticism toward a claim, common in news reporting.

examples.target: Il semble fatigué ce matin.
examples.translation_tr: He seems tired this morning.
examples.note_tr: sembler + adjective, direct impression based on appearance.

examples.target: Il semble qu'il y ait un problème.
examples.translation_tr: It seems (that) there is a problem.
examples.note_tr: Impersonal 'il semble que' with no dative pronoun expresses doubt, so it takes the subjunctive (ait).

examples.target: Il me semble que vous avez raison.
examples.translation_tr: It seems to me that you are right.
examples.note_tr: Adding the dative pronoun (me) turns this into a personal, near-certain opinion, so the indicative (avez) is used.

examples.target: Elle paraît plus jeune que son âge.
examples.translation_tr: She looks/appears younger than her age.
examples.note_tr: paraître + adjective describing visible, objective appearance.

examples.target: Il paraît qu'ils vont déménager.
examples.translation_tr: Apparently, they are moving.
examples.note_tr: 'il paraît que' always takes the indicative and signals hearsay/rumor, not personal opinion.

examples.target: Il doit être tard, le ciel est déjà sombre.
examples.translation_tr: It must be late, the sky is already dark.
examples.note_tr: Epistemic devoir (present tense) expresses strong logical probability, not obligation.

examples.target: Il devrait avoir fini son travail à cette heure-ci.
examples.translation_tr: He should have finished his work by now.
examples.note_tr: Conditional devoir + past infinitive = softened expectation about a completed action (epistemic, not a reproach).

examples.target: On dirait qu'il va pleuvoir.
examples.translation_tr: It looks like it's going to rain.
examples.note_tr: on dirait que + indicative: a sensory/visual impression, very common in spoken French.

word-formation.title_tr: Word Formation (Prefixes and Suffixes: re-, dé-, -able, -eur)
word-formation.intro_tr: French is highly productive with derivational morphology: a small set of prefixes and suffixes lets you generate whole families of words from a single root. The prefixes re-/ré-/r- ("again") and dé-/dés- ("undo, remove, reverse") attach mainly to verbs and change their meaning without changing their word class. The suffixes -able/-ible and -eur/-euse (or -teur/-trice) attach to verb or adjective stems and change the word class: -able/-ible turns a verb into an adjective meaning "capable of being ...-ed", while -eur/-euse turns a verb into an agent noun ("the person/thing that does X") or an adjective into an abstract quality noun. Knowing these patterns lets you guess or build unfamiliar vocabulary instead of memorizing every word individually. Spelling of the prefix (re- vs ré- vs r-, dé- vs dés-) depends on whether the base word starts with a consonant or a vowel, and the suffix -able/-ible and -eur have several irregular or historically French/Latin-derived forms that must be learned as exceptions.

tables.caption_tr: Prefix re- / ré- / r-; repetition or reinforcement ('again')
rows: to go back in, come home
footnotes_tr: There is no single fixed rule for ré- vs r- before a vowel; both exist and must often be learned per verb (rouvrir but réécrire).
re- can also intensify or reinforce a meaning rather than strictly repeat it, e.g. remplir (to fill up) from emplir.

tables.caption_tr: Prefix dé- / dés-; reversal, removal, or negation of an action
footnotes_tr: dés- is used before a vowel sound mainly to keep the base word's spelling/pronunciation clear and avoid an awkward vowel cluster.

tables.caption_tr: Suffix -able / -ible; adjectives meaning 'able to be ...-ed'
rows: many -ible words are borrowed directly, not derived
footnotes_tr: Adding the negative prefix in-/im- to -able/-ible words is very common: mangeable → immangeable (inedible), croyable → incroyable (unbelievable), lisible → illisible (illegible).

tables.caption_tr: Suffix -eur / -euse / -teur / -trice; agent nouns ('the person/thing that does X')
footnotes_tr: Verbs in -er usually take -eur/-euse; many Latinate or -ire/-uire verbs take -teur/-trice instead.
A few common exceptions keep the same form for both genders, e.g. un/une élève is not from this pattern but shows gender isn't always marked by suffix change.

tables.caption_tr: Suffix -eur on adjectives; abstract quality nouns (not people)
footnotes_tr: All nouns formed this way from adjectives are feminine, unlike agent nouns in -eur which are masculine (feminine counterpart is -euse/-trice).

tables.caption_tr: Other frequent prefixes for reference
footnotes_tr: The negative prefix in- assimilates to the following consonant: im- before b/m/p (impossible), il- before l (illisible), ir- before r (irrégulier).

tables.caption_tr: Other frequent suffixes for reference
footnotes_tr: -tion/-age/-ment (nominalization) and -ment (adverb formation) are large enough topics to have their own dedicated grammar pages.

examples.target: Je dois refaire mes devoirs, ils sont pleins de fautes.
examples.translation_tr: I have to redo my homework, it's full of mistakes.
examples.note_tr: re- + faire → refaire (repetition)

examples.target: Elle va réécrire son article avant de le publier.
examples.translation_tr: She is going to rewrite her article before publishing it.
examples.note_tr: ré- used before a vowel-initial verb (écrire)

examples.target: Peux-tu défaire ce nœud, s'il te plaît ?
examples.translation_tr: Can you undo this knot, please?
examples.note_tr: dé- + faire → défaire (reversal of an action)

examples.target: Il faut se déshabiller avant d'entrer dans la piscine.
examples.translation_tr: You must undress before entering the pool.
examples.note_tr: dés- used before a vowel-initial verb (habiller)

examples.target: Ce texte est difficilement lisible sans mes lunettes.
examples.translation_tr: This text is hardly readable without my glasses.
examples.note_tr: lire → lisible, irregular -ible stem

examples.target: C'est un problème facilement compréhensible.
examples.translation_tr: It's an easily understandable problem.
examples.note_tr: comprendre → compréhensible

examples.target: Le chanteur et la chanteuse ont donné un excellent concert hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: The (male) singer and the (female) singer gave an excellent concert last night.
examples.note_tr: -eur/-euse agent noun pair from chanter

examples.target: La grandeur de ce projet impressionne tout le monde.
examples.translation_tr: The scale of this project impresses everyone.
examples.note_tr: grand → grandeur, abstract quality noun with -eur

punctuation-style.title_tr: Fine Points of French Punctuation and Typography (dashes, guillemets, spacing rules)
punctuation-style.intro_tr: French typography follows stricter and more visually distinct rules than English, and mastering them is a hallmark of polished written French. Three separate marks exist where English uses one dash: the short trait d'union for compound words, the medium tiret (en dash) for ranges and asides, and the long tiret cadratin (em dash) for dialogue. French also inserts a space before double-component punctuation marks (: ; ! ? and the guillemets « »), always using a non-breaking space so the mark never gets stranded at the start of a line. Quotation is handled with guillemets « » rather than "curly quotes," and numbers swap the roles of comma and period compared to English. This page collects the spacing, dash, quotation, and number-formatting rules a C1 writer is expected to apply automatically.

tables.caption_tr: Spacing before punctuation marks (French vs. English)
rows: Voici la liste : pain, lait, œufs.
Il fait froid ; je reste chez moi.
footnotes_tr: The 'non-breaking space' used before ; : ! ? and inside « » is technically a narrow non-breaking space (espace fine insécable); its purpose is to prevent the punctuation mark from being separated from its word or from starting a new line.

Many word processors and websites substitute a regular non-breaking space (or even a normal space) when the narrow version isn't available; both are acceptable in everyday typing, but professional typesetting uses the narrow one.

tables.caption_tr: Guillemets « »; French quotation marks
rows: « ... » with non-breaking spaces just inside the marks
Il a dit : « Je reviens demain. »
Nested quotation (a quote inside a quote)
Inner quote uses straight double quotes " " inside the outer « »
Outer double quotes, inner single quotes ' '
Usually set in italics in formal print; guillemets used informally or in handwriting
J'ai lu Le Petit Prince (formal) / « Le Petit Prince » (informal)
Highlighting or distancing a word (irony, jargon)
« mot » with a comma or period placed outside the closing guillemet
Il est « gentil », si on peut dire.
Colon + guillemets (no comma before the colon-quote combo)
footnotes_tr: Unlike English, French normally places the closing guillemet before trailing punctuation that belongs to the surrounding sentence, not the quoted words themselves.

tables.caption_tr: The three hyphen/dash marks: trait d'union, tiret demi-cadratin, tiret cadratin
rows: Compound words; inverted question forms; compound numbers under 100
Numeric or date ranges; light parenthetical insertion; connecting two related terms
Marking a change of speaker in dialogue; strong parenthetical break in a sentence
; Tu viens ?; Oui, j'arrive.; Ce livre; le meilleur de l'année; mérite d'être lu.
footnotes_tr: Standard keyboards do not have dedicated en/em dash keys; word processors often auto-correct a double hyphen (--) into the appropriate dash, or you can insert the Unicode characters directly (– U+2013; U+2014).

tables.caption_tr: Formatting spoken dialogue with tirets cadratins (, )
rows: Guillemets « » may frame the whole conversation; each new speaker's turn begins with a tiret cadratin
Start a new paragraph/line with; for every new speaker; no quotation marks are needed around each individual line
A second tiret (usually shorter, –) sets off the narrator's comment within the same line of dialogue
; Je ne sais pas, dit-elle; si tu viens vraiment.
If guillemets were used to open the whole dialogue, the closing » appears only after the final line
footnotes_tr: Contemporary French fiction increasingly uses tirets alone (without surrounding guillemets) for entire dialogue passages; both styles are considered correct.

tables.caption_tr: Number and currency formatting conventions
rows: Superscript letters after the digit, no period

tables.caption_tr: Frequent English-to-French typography mistakes
rows: Guillemets are the standard French quotation mark
Insert a (narrow) non-breaking space before these marks
French treats them as two-part symbols needing separation from the text
Use comma only for decimals; use a space for thousands
The roles of comma and period are swapped relative to English
1 000,50 means one thousand point five zero
Capitalizing every major word in a title
Capitalize only the first word and proper nouns
French title case is far less aggressive than English
Le Petit Prince, not Le Petit Prince style caps on every word
Using a plain hyphen (-) for everything
Choose the correct dash for the function: - for compounds, – for ranges; for dialogue
Each mark signals a distinct grammatical or stylistic role
vingt-deux vs. pages 10–15 vs.; Tu viens ?

examples.target: « Bonjour ! » a-t-elle dit avec un grand sourire.
examples.translation_tr: "Hello!" she said with a big smile.

examples.target: Il fait très froid ; je préfère rester à la maison.
examples.translation_tr: It's very cold; I'd rather stay home.

examples.target: ; Tu viens ce soir ?; Oui, avec plaisir.
examples.translation_tr: "Are you coming tonight?"; "Yes, gladly."

examples.translation_tr: The total price is €25.50 for 1,000 copies.

examples.translation_tr: The Paris–Lyon journey takes about two hours.

examples.target: « Il m'a répondu : "Je reviens tout de suite." »
examples.translation_tr: "He answered me: 'I'll be right back.'"
